references.label: Kocher MS et al. Differentiating between septic arthritis and transient synovitis of the hip. JBJS 1999

title: Paediatric cancer — NG12 red flag referral pathway
description: Refer for immediate (within 48 h) paediatric assessment if any of: unexplained petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly, persistent lymphadenopathy with concerning features, mass arising from any soft tissue or bone, persistent unexplained bone pain, persistent localised back pain, persistent headaches with morning vomiting, new neurological signs, suspected retinoblastoma (leucocoria/squint with red reflex loss), unexplained weight loss with night sweats.

outcomes.summary: Paediatric red flag for cancer — 48 h referral
outcomes.detail: Petechiae/hepatosplenomegaly/abdominal mass/leucocoria/persistent unexplained bone pain — urgent referral.

references.label: NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral 2015 (updated)

title: Paediatric IV paracetamol — weight-based dose ceiling
description: IV paracetamol in children: 15 mg/kg every 6 h (max 60 mg/kg/day, not exceeding 4 g). Reduce to 7.5 mg/kg every 6 h (max 30 mg/kg/day) in neonates <10 kg, hepatic impairment, malnutrition or weight <50 kg adolescents at higher risk. Do not give >15 mg/kg in a single dose. Wrong-route paracetamol overdose (oral dose given IV) is a known incident — double-check route, dose and weight at prescribing and administration.

outcomes.summary: IV paracetamol — weight-banded, max 60 mg/kg/day
outcomes.detail: Reduce in neonates, malnutrition, hepatic impairment; double-check route at administration.

references.label: MHRA Drug Safety Update: Paracetamol intravenous infusion — risk of accidental overdose 2010
BNF for Children 2024

title: Pre-eclampsia prevention — low-dose aspirin from 12 weeks
description: Offer aspirin 75-150 mg once daily from 12 weeks until birth in women with one HIGH risk factor (hypertensive disease in previous pregnancy, chronic kidney disease, autoimmune disease (SLE, APS), type 1 or 2 diabetes, chronic hypertension) OR more than one MODERATE risk factor (first pregnancy, age ≥40, BMI ≥35 at booking, family history pre-eclampsia, multiple pregnancy, interpregnancy interval >10 years).

outcomes.summary: High/moderate-risk pregnancy — aspirin 75-150 mg from 12 weeks
outcomes.detail: Continue until birth; review by booking midwife and obstetrician.

references.label: NICE NG133 Hypertension in pregnancy: diagnosis and management 2019 (updated)
Rolnik DL et al. Aspirin versus Placebo in Pregnancies at High Risk for Preterm Preeclampsia (ASPRE). NEJM 2017

title: Eclampsia and severe pre-eclampsia — magnesium sulfate
description: For eclamptic seizure or severe pre-eclampsia (BP ≥160/110 with proteinuria/end-organ involvement) give magnesium sulfate IV loading dose 4 g over 5-15 minutes, followed by maintenance infusion 1 g/h for 24 hours after the last seizure or delivery (whichever later). Pritchard IM alternative: 4 g IV + 10 g IM (5 g each buttock), then 5 g IM every 4 hours. Monitor patellar reflex hourly, respiratory rate (>16/min), urine output (>30 mL/h). Antidote: 10% calcium gluconate 10 mL slow IV for toxicity.

outcomes.summary: Eclampsia/severe PE — magnesium sulfate now
outcomes.detail: Loading 4 g IV + maintenance 1 g/h for 24 h post-seizure or delivery; monitor reflexes, RR, UO.

references.label: WHO recommendations for prevention and treatment of pre-eclampsia and eclampsia 2011
Altman D et al. (Magpie Trial). Lancet 2002

title: Gestational diabetes — 75 g OGTT screening at 24-28 weeks
description: Screen with 75 g OGTT at 24-28 weeks in all women with risk factors (BMI ≥30, previous macrosomic baby ≥4.5 kg, previous GDM, family history of diabetes, ethnic minority high-risk). Diagnose GDM by IADPSG/WHO 2013: fasting ≥5.1 mmol/L, 1-h ≥10.0 mmol/L, or 2-h ≥8.5 mmol/L. Lifestyle first for 1-2 weeks; if targets not met (fasting <5.3, 1-h post-meal <7.8, 2-h <6.4) add metformin then insulin. Postnatal OGTT or fasting glucose at 6-13 weeks; annual HbA1c thereafter.

outcomes.summary: GDM diagnosed — diet/exercise first, escalate to metformin/insulin
outcomes.detail: Postnatal glucose at 6-13 weeks and annual HbA1c thereafter.

references.label: NICE NG3 Diabetes in pregnancy 2015 (updated 2020)
WHO Diagnostic criteria and classification of hyperglycaemia first detected in pregnancy 2013

title: Postpartum haemorrhage — E-MOTIVE first-response bundle
description: Define PPH as blood loss ≥500 mL after vaginal birth or ≥1000 mL after caesarean, or any loss causing haemodynamic instability. E-MOTIVE bundle: Early detection (calibrated drape), Massage uterus, Oxytocin 10 IU IM/IV, Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours, IV fluids, Examination of birth canal/escalation. WOMAN trial: TXA reduces maternal death from bleeding when given early. Continue active management: ergometrine 0.5 mg IM (avoid if hypertensive), carboprost 0.25 mg IM, misoprostol 800 mcg sublingual where parenteral unavailable, balloon tamponade, B-Lynch suture, hysterectomy.

outcomes.summary: PPH — E-MOTIVE bundle within minutes; TXA within 3 h
outcomes.detail: Calibrated drape, massage, oxytocin, TXA 1 g IV, fluids, escalate; continue uterotonics ladder.

references.label: WHO E-MOTIVE trial Lancet 2023; WHO recommendations on the management of postpartum haemorrhage 2024
WOMAN Trial Collaborators. Lancet 2017

title: Antenatal/postnatal VTE risk — RCOG Green-top 37a
description: Score VTE risk at booking and after every admission. Antenatal: ≥4 points before 28 weeks → LMWH from first trimester; ≥3 points from 28 weeks → LMWH from 28 weeks. Postnatal: ≥2 points → LMWH 10 days; previous VTE, antithrombin deficiency, ≥3 risk factors → 6 weeks. Risk factors: previous VTE, thrombophilia, age ≥35, BMI ≥30, parity ≥3, smoker, gross varicose veins, multiple pregnancy, IVF, immobility, PE/PIH, surgery, sickle cell. Avoid DOACs in pregnancy/breastfeeding; warfarin contraindicated in pregnancy.

outcomes.summary: Pregnancy VTE risk score — apply RCOG Green-top 37a
outcomes.detail: Reassess after every admission; LMWH dose by booking weight.

references.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 37a Reducing the Risk of Venous Thromboembolism during Pregnancy and the Puerperium 2015

title: Group B Strep — intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis criteria
description: Offer intrapartum benzylpenicillin (initial 3 g IV then 1.5 g every 4 h until delivery) in: previous baby with GBS disease, GBS bacteriuria this pregnancy, GBS carriage detected in current pregnancy, preterm labour <37 weeks, intrapartum fever ≥38°C, prolonged rupture of membranes ≥18 h at term. Penicillin allergy without anaphylaxis — cefazolin 2 g then 1 g every 8 h; severe penicillin allergy — vancomycin (after sensitivity testing where possible).

outcomes.summary: GBS risk factor — benzylpenicillin intrapartum
outcomes.detail: Continue 4-hourly until delivery; cefazolin or vancomycin if penicillin-allergic.

references.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 36 Prevention of Early-onset Neonatal Group B Streptococcal Disease 2017

codings.display: Other maternal infectious and parasitic diseases

title: Postnatal depression — EPDS screening at 6-8 weeks
description: Administer Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) at the 6-8 week postnatal review (and at 3-4 months in some pathways). Score ≥10 — clinical assessment for depression; ≥13 — likely depression, initiate treatment. Always review item 10 (self-harm thoughts): positive → same-day mental health assessment. Treatment: psychological therapy (CBT/IPT) first-line for mild-moderate; sertraline preferred in breastfeeding (low levels in milk); avoid paroxetine in late pregnancy.

outcomes.summary: EPDS ≥10 — clinical assessment; ≥13 — start treatment
outcomes.detail: Any positive self-harm item triggers same-day mental health assessment.

references.label: NICE CG192 Antenatal and postnatal mental health 2014 (updated 2020)

title: Postpartum contraception — counselling and timing
description: Discuss contraception in the postnatal period before discharge from maternity. Progestogen-only methods (POP, implant, depot, LNG-IUS, copper IUD) safe immediately postpartum and during breastfeeding. Combined hormonal contraception NOT for breastfeeding women in first 6 weeks (VTE risk and milk supply), avoid until 6 weeks postpartum. Intrauterine devices may be inserted immediately post-placenta or after 4 weeks. LAM only effective if exclusive breastfeeding, amenorrhoeic, <6 months. Offer immediate post-placental IUD or postpartum implant as part of PMTCT contact.

outcomes.summary: Discuss postpartum contraception before discharge
outcomes.detail: POPs/implants/IUDs safe immediately; CHC avoided in first 6 weeks especially if breastfeeding.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use 2015
FSRH Postnatal Sexual and Reproductive Health 2017

title: Maternal sepsis — 1-hour bundle (RCOG Green-top 64)
description: Suspect maternal sepsis in pregnancy or up to 42 days postpartum with infection plus organ dysfunction or qSOFA ≥2. Within 1 hour: oxygen for SpO2 <94% (88-92% in COPD), blood cultures and other site cultures, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g, or amoxicillin + gentamicin + metronidazole), IV crystalloid 30 mL/kg, measure lactate, monitor urine output. Consider sources unique to obstetrics: chorioamnionitis, endometritis, mastitis, wound, retained products. Group A Strep is the leading cause; rapid antibiotics save lives.

outcomes.summary: Maternal sepsis — 1-hour bundle now
outcomes.detail: Cultures, antibiotics, fluids, lactate within 1 h; consider obstetric-specific sources.

references.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 64a Bacterial Sepsis in Pregnancy 2012

title: Stillbirth — investigation pathway and bereavement care
description: After stillbirth offer a parental-led investigation pathway. Core investigations: post-mortem (full or limited per parental consent), placental histology and culture, fetal/maternal karyotype, microarray, Kleihauer, maternal infection screen (CMV, parvovirus, toxoplasma, syphilis, listeria), thrombophilia per RCOG, HbA1c, autoantibodies, full blood count, urine toxicology if indicated. Provide structured bereavement care, lactation suppression discussion, contraception, and follow-up appointment with results within 12 weeks. Notify confidential enquiry where applicable.

outcomes.summary: Stillbirth investigations — placental histology + bloods + parental-led decisions
outcomes.detail: Offer post-mortem; arrange bereavement support and 12-week follow-up.

references.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 55 Late Intrauterine Fetal Death and Stillbirth 2010
MBRRACE-UK Perinatal Confidential Enquiries

title: Anti-D immunoglobulin — routine antenatal and sensitising events
description: In RhD-negative women without anti-D antibodies give routine anti-D as either 1500 IU at 28 weeks (single-dose regimen) or 500 IU at 28 and 34 weeks (two-dose regimen). After any potentially sensitising event (abdominal trauma, threatened miscarriage ≥12 weeks, ectopic pregnancy, evacuation of molar/missed miscarriage, amniocentesis/CVS, ECV, antepartum haemorrhage) give 250 IU before 20 weeks and 500 IU after 20 weeks with Kleihauer to quantify FMH. Postnatal: 500 IU within 72 hours of birth of an RhD-positive infant.

outcomes.summary: RhD-negative — anti-D for routine and sensitising events
outcomes.detail: Postnatal anti-D within 72 h of delivery of RhD-positive baby; quantify FMH after >20 weeks events.

references.label: BCSH Guideline for the use of anti-D immunoglobulin for the prevention of haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn 2014

title: Pregnancy and heart disease — modified WHO risk classification
description: Stratify maternal cardiac risk using modified WHO classification. mWHO I — no detectable increased risk. mWHO II — slightly increased risk (most unoperated atrial/ventricular septal defects, repaired tetralogy of Fallot). mWHO II-III — moderately increased risk (mild LV impairment, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, native or tissue valve disease not in mWHO IV). mWHO III — significantly increased risk (mechanical valve, systemic right ventricle, Fontan, cyanotic heart disease, moderate LV impairment). mWHO IV — pregnancy contraindicated (pulmonary arterial hypertension, severe systemic ventricular dysfunction, severe left heart obstruction, severe aortic dilatation). Refer all to joint cardio-obstetric MDT.

outcomes.summary: Pregnancy + heart disease — refer cardio-obstetric MDT, mWHO class
outcomes.detail: mWHO IV — counsel against pregnancy or for termination; mWHO III — tertiary centre delivery.

references.label: ESC Guidelines for the management of cardiovascular diseases during pregnancy 2018

codings.display: Diseases of the circulatory system complicating pregnancy

title: HELLP syndrome — recognition and definitive management
description: HELLP: Haemolysis (LDH ≥600 IU/L, schistocytes on film), Elevated Liver enzymes (AST ≥70 IU/L), Low Platelets (<100 × 10⁹/L), in pregnancy or postpartum, usually but not always with hypertension. Definitive management is DELIVERY when ≥34 weeks or maternal/fetal compromise; consider 48 h steroids for fetal lung maturity if 24-34 weeks and stable. Concurrent control of BP (labetalol/nifedipine), magnesium sulfate, platelet transfusion if <20 × 10⁹/L (or <50 if surgery), correct coagulopathy. HDU/ICU.

outcomes.summary: HELLP — deliver if ≥34 weeks or compromise
outcomes.detail: BP control, magnesium, steroids for lung maturity if 24-34 weeks, platelet transfusion thresholds.

references.label: NICE NG133 Hypertension in pregnancy 2019
RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 10A 2018

title: Pregnancy and epilepsy — high-dose folate and AED selection
description: Pre-conception or as early as possible: folic acid 5 mg daily continued throughout pregnancy. AED counselling: AVOID sodium valproate in women/girls of childbearing potential except under Pregnancy Prevention Programme; carbamazepine and phenytoin associated with neural tube defects. Lamotrigine and levetiracetam have lowest known teratogenic risk among older AEDs. Continue most effective regimen at lowest effective dose; check AED levels regularly (especially lamotrigine — clearance increases in pregnancy). Vitamin K to the neonate; encourage breastfeeding; register on UK Epilepsy and Pregnancy Register.

outcomes.summary: Epilepsy in pregnancy — folate 5 mg, avoid valproate
outcomes.detail: Lamotrigine/levetiracetam preferred; AED levels regularly; register on epilepsy and pregnancy register.

references.label: MHRA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Programme 2018 (updated)
NICE NG217 Epilepsies in children, young people and adults 2022

title: Hyperemesis gravidarum — PUQE scoring and management ladder
description: Score nausea and vomiting in pregnancy with PUQE: mild ≤6, moderate 7-12, severe ≥13. Step 1: oral cyclizine 50 mg TDS or promethazine 25 mg TDS; pyridoxine + doxylamine option. Step 2: oral ondansetron 4-8 mg TDS (counsel re cleft lip data — shared decision after 12 weeks preferable) or metoclopramide 5-10 mg TDS (avoid >5 days due to extrapyramidal). Step 3: IV fluids (normal saline + KCl), parenteral antiemetics, corticosteroids (hydrocortisone 100 mg BD then taper). Always: thiamine to prevent Wernicke's before any glucose, VTE prophylaxis if dehydrated/admitted.

outcomes.summary: HG admission — IV fluids + thiamine + VTE prophylaxis
outcomes.detail: Thiamine before any dextrose; PUQE ≥13 — admit; step-up antiemetics; check ketones, weight, U&E.

references.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 69 The Management of Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy and Hyperemesis Gravidarum 2024 update

title: Pre-conception folic acid 5 mg — high-risk groups
description: Recommend folic acid 5 mg daily from pre-conception until 12 weeks gestation in high-risk groups: previous pregnancy with neural tube defect, family history NTD, diabetes mellitus, BMI ≥30, sickle cell or thalassaemia, coeliac disease, on AEDs (especially valproate, carbamazepine, phenytoin). All other women: 400 mcg daily from pre-conception to 12 weeks.

outcomes.summary: Pre-conception folate 5 mg in high-risk groups
outcomes.detail: Other women: 400 mcg daily; continue to 12 weeks.

references.label: NICE Antenatal care NG201 2021

codings.display: Encounter for procreative investigation and testing

title: Postpartum thyroiditis — recognition and follow-up
description: Up to 8% of women develop postpartum thyroiditis within 12 months. Triphasic pattern: thyrotoxicosis (1-6 months) → hypothyroidism (3-12 months) → recovery. Thyrotoxic phase usually mild — beta-blocker for symptoms; do NOT use antithyroid drugs (destruction not overproduction). Hypothyroid phase — levothyroxine if symptomatic, TSH >10, or attempting pregnancy. Annual TSH thereafter — 20-40% develop permanent hypothyroidism. Higher risk in TPO-positive, type 1 diabetes, prior postpartum thyroiditis.

outcomes.summary: Postpartum thyroiditis — symptomatic treatment; annual TSH
outcomes.detail: Do not use ATD in thyrotoxic phase; levothyroxine in hypothyroid phase if symptomatic.

references.label: ATA Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Thyroid Disease During Pregnancy and the Postpartum 2017

title: Pregnancy and HIV — ART for vertical transmission prevention
description: All pregnant women with HIV should be on lifelong ART (dolutegravir-based regimen preferred per WHO 2021). Aim for undetectable viral load by 36 weeks. Mode of delivery: vaginal birth if VL <50 copies/mL at 36 weeks; planned caesarean at 38+ weeks if VL >50 or unknown. Intrapartum IV zidovudine for VL ≥1000 copies/mL. Neonate: zidovudine monotherapy for low-risk, triple-drug prophylaxis (AZT + 3TC + NVP) for high-risk, for 4-6 weeks. Avoid breastfeeding only if formula AFASS criteria met; otherwise continue exclusive breastfeeding with maternal ART per WHO PMTCT.

outcomes.summary: Pregnancy + HIV — lifelong ART, VL by 36 weeks decides delivery
outcomes.detail: DTG-based ART preferred; intrapartum AZT if VL ≥1000; infant prophylaxis 4-6 weeks.

references.label: WHO Consolidated guidelines on HIV 2021
BHIVA Guidelines for the management of HIV in pregnancy and postpartum 2020

title: First trimester combined screening — nuchal translucency, PAPP-A, free β-hCG
description: Offer combined test between 11+2 and 14+1 weeks: maternal age, NT measurement, PAPP-A, free β-hCG. Reports risk for trisomies 21, 18, 13. Risk threshold ≥1:150 — offer cfDNA (NIPT) as contingent screening or invasive diagnostic (CVS 11-14 wks, amniocentesis ≥15 wks). Women presenting >14 weeks: offer quadruple test 14+2 to 20+0 weeks. Counsel about miscarriage risks of invasive testing (~0.5%) and the limitations of screening tests.

outcomes.summary: Combined screening 11+2 to 14+1 weeks
outcomes.detail: cfDNA contingent on high-risk result; offer invasive diagnostic if requested.

references.label: UK NHS Fetal Anomaly Screening Programme Handbook 2024

codings.display: Encounter for antenatal screening for chromosomal anomalies

title: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia — antenatal management and delivery
description: Major placenta praevia (covering os) confirmed on TVUS at 32 weeks: plan elective caesarean at 36+0 to 37+0 weeks. Anaesthetic, blood bank, and consultant obstetrician staffing. Antenatal corticosteroids if delivery 24-34+6 weeks anticipated; consider magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection <32 weeks. Vasa praevia: plan delivery 34-36 weeks by caesarean; consider antenatal admission from 30-32 weeks; betamethasone for lung maturity. Suspect placenta accreta spectrum if previous CS plus anterior low placenta — MRI for invasion depth; deliver in tertiary unit.

outcomes.summary: Major praevia — elective CS 36-37 weeks; vasa praevia — 34-36 weeks
outcomes.detail: Antenatal steroids if preterm anticipated; PAS suspected in previous CS + anterior low placenta.

references.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 27a Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta 2018
RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 27b Vasa Praevia 2018

title: DKA in pregnancy — modified protocol with fetal monitoring
description: DKA in pregnancy can occur at lower glucose levels (euglycaemic DKA). Treat per usual DKA protocol (fixed-rate insulin 0.1 U/kg/h, normal saline initially, K+ replacement) but: monitor fetus continuously where viable; obstetrician and physician joint care; correct slowly to minimise risk of cerebral oedema; left lateral tilt; aggressive fluid resuscitation may risk pulmonary oedema in pre-eclampsia, monitor closely. Do NOT deliver until maternally stable unless fetal distress not resolving — delivery often improves DKA but maternal stabilisation comes first.

outcomes.summary: DKA in pregnancy — joint obstetric/medical care, stabilise mother first
outcomes.detail: Euglycaemic DKA possible; continuous fetal monitoring; deliver only if stable or persistent fetal distress.

references.label: JBDS-IP Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care: Management of DKA in adults 2023; DKA in pregnancy considerations

title: Reduced fetal movements — RCOG Green-top 57 pathway
description: For women ≥28 weeks presenting with reduced fetal movements: take history, abdominal palpation, auscultate FH, CTG for ≥20 min. If normal — reassure; advise to monitor and re-attend if reduced again. If CTG abnormal or persistent maternal concern — ultrasound within 24 h (growth, liquor volume, umbilical Doppler). Two or more episodes of RFM — senior obstetric review; consider induction if at term and any concern. Do not formally use kick counts; women should report any concerning change.

outcomes.summary: RFM ≥28 weeks — CTG; US within 24 h if any abnormality
outcomes.detail: Two or more episodes — senior review and consider induction at term.

references.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 57 Reduced Fetal Movements 2011 (under review)

title: Chronic hypertension in pregnancy — antihypertensive selection
description: Discontinue ACE inhibitors, ARBs, thiazides (chlorothiazide preserved for indication), and renin inhibitors immediately on pregnancy confirmation. Target BP <135/85 mmHg in chronic and gestational hypertension. First-line: labetalol 200-1200 mg/day in divided doses (avoid in asthma). Alternatives: nifedipine MR 20-90 mg/day, methyldopa 250-500 mg TDS (legacy, more side effects). Aspirin 75-150 mg from 12 weeks for pre-eclampsia prophylaxis. Postpartum: avoid methyldopa (depression), continue/switch to enalapril if breastfeeding (compatible).

outcomes.summary: Chronic HTN pregnancy — stop ACE/ARB, start labetalol/nifedipine
outcomes.detail: Target <135/85; aspirin from 12 weeks; switch to enalapril if breastfeeding.

references.label: NICE NG133 Hypertension in pregnancy 2019 update
CHIPS Trial. NEJM 2015

title: Antenatal corticosteroids — 24+0 to 34+6 weeks
description: Offer single course of antenatal corticosteroids to women at risk of preterm delivery 24+0 to 34+6 weeks: betamethasone 12 mg IM, two doses 24 h apart (or dexamethasone 6 mg IM × 4 doses 12 h apart). Discuss with patient if 35+0 to 36+6 weeks and planning birth within 7 days (modest neonatal benefit). Repeat course only if first course >7 days ago AND continued high risk AND <34+0. Single rescue dose may be used in select circumstances.

outcomes.summary: Anticipated preterm 24-34+6 weeks — single course of antenatal steroids
outcomes.detail: Betamethasone 12 mg IM × 2 doses 24 h apart; dexamethasone alternative.

references.label: NICE NG25 Preterm labour and birth 2015 (updated 2022)
WHO ACTION-I Trial Lancet 2020

title: Magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection <30 weeks
description: Offer magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection in established preterm labour or planned preterm birth within 24 h, between 24+0 and 29+6 weeks. Loading: 4 g IV over 20-30 minutes; maintenance: 1 g/h until birth or up to 24 h, whichever sooner. Monitor maternal reflexes, RR, urine output. Reduces risk of cerebral palsy and gross motor dysfunction in survivors.

outcomes.summary: <30 weeks imminent preterm — magnesium for neuroprotection
outcomes.detail: Loading 4 g over 20-30 min then 1 g/h to birth or 24 h.

references.label: NICE NG25 Preterm labour and birth 2015 (updated 2022)
Doyle LW et al. (Cochrane) Magnesium sulphate for women at risk of preterm birth for neuroprotection of the fetus 2009

title: Breastfeeding — medication compatibility check
description: For any medicine prescribed to a breastfeeding mother check LactMed/UKDILAS before counselling. Compatible defaults: paracetamol, ibuprofen, most penicillins/cephalosporins/macrolides (avoid prolonged trimethoprim in jaundiced neonate), sertraline (preferred SSRI), labetalol, nifedipine, enalapril. Avoid or use with caution: codeine and tramadol (CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metabolisers — risk to infant; MHRA advise avoid), aspirin >75 mg, lithium, amiodarone, retinoids, chemotherapy, ergot derivatives, radioactive iodine.

outcomes.summary: Breastfeeding — check LactMed/UKDILAS before prescribing
outcomes.detail: Avoid codeine/tramadol/lithium/amiodarone/chemo/retinoids/radioactive iodine.

references.label: MHRA Drug Safety Update: Codeine for analgesia: restricted use in children because of reports of morphine toxicity 2013
LactMed (NIH) breastfeeding drug database

codings.display: Encounter for care and examination of lactating mother

title: Cervical cerclage — history-, ultrasound-, and physical-indicated
description: History-indicated cerclage at 12-14 weeks: ≥3 previous preterm births and/or second-trimester losses. Ultrasound-indicated cerclage: shortened cervix <25 mm on TVUS between 16 and 24 weeks with previous spontaneous preterm birth <34 weeks. Physical examination–indicated (rescue) cerclage: dilated cervix or membranes visible at the os 16-27+6 weeks without infection or labour, after counselling. Vaginal progesterone 200 mg pessary daily is an alternative for short cervix without history of preterm birth.

outcomes.summary: Consider cerclage for history/US/exam indications
outcomes.detail: Vaginal progesterone alternative for short cervix without preterm history.

references.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 60 Cervical Cerclage 2011

title: Shoulder dystocia — HELPERR manoeuvres
description: Call for help. Evaluate for episiotomy. Legs (McRoberts). Pressure (suprapubic, not fundal). Enter pelvis (Rubin/Wood's/reverse Wood's screw). Remove posterior arm. Roll over to all fours (Gaskin). Document time of head delivery, manoeuvres used, time to body delivery. Risk: brachial plexus injury, fracture clavicle/humerus, hypoxic injury, PPH, perineal trauma. Debrief with parents and team.

outcomes.summary: Shoulder dystocia — HELPERR sequence
outcomes.detail: McRoberts first; suprapubic not fundal pressure; document times and manoeuvres.

references.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 42 Shoulder Dystocia 2012

codings.display: Obstructed labour due to shoulder dystocia

title: PPROM <34 weeks — expectant management with surveillance
description: Confirm PPROM by speculum (pooling) or commercial test (AmniSure/Actim PROM) if equivocal. Expectant management if <34 weeks: erythromycin 250 mg QDS for 10 days (or until birth), antenatal corticosteroids, magnesium sulfate <30 weeks, daily CTG, twice-weekly bloods (WCC, CRP), USS for growth. Deliver at 34+0 if previously stable. Group B Strep prophylaxis on entry into labour. Chorioamnionitis (maternal fever, tachycardia, fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness, offensive discharge) — deliver irrespective of gestation, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics.

outcomes.summary: PPROM <34 weeks — erythromycin + steroids + magnesium; deliver at 34
outcomes.detail: Deliver any gestation if chorioamnionitis develops.

references.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 73 Care of Women Presenting with Suspected Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes from 24+0 Weeks of Gestation 2019

title: Amniotic fluid embolism — recognition and resuscitation
description: Suspect AFE in any peripartum woman with sudden cardiovascular collapse, hypoxia, and disseminated intravascular coagulation, often with profound hypotension or cardiac arrest. Resuscitate per ALS with left lateral tilt; if no ROSC by 4 minutes deliver baby (perimortem caesarean). Massive transfusion protocol activation, fibrinogen replacement (cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate), tranexamic acid. Atypical antifibrinolytic-resistant coagulopathy may require recombinant factor VIIa as last resort. ITU-level care.

outcomes.summary: AFE — ALS, perimortem CS by 4 min if no ROSC, MTP
outcomes.detail: Fibrinogen replacement aggressive; ITU-level care; declare clinical emergency to whole team.

references.label: RCOG/AAGBI/OAA Maternal Collapse in Pregnancy and the Puerperium Green-top Guideline No. 56 2019

title: Maternal cardiac arrest — perimortem caesarean by 4 minutes
description: In maternal cardiac arrest with gestation ≥20 weeks (uterine fundus at or above umbilicus) perform left uterine displacement (manual or 15° tilt), start CPR with hands slightly higher on sternum, ensure airway, and prepare for perimortem caesarean delivery by 4 minutes from arrest if no ROSC. The procedure is for maternal benefit (relieves aortocaval compression) — do not delay for transfer to theatre. Whole team must be ready; do not wait for senior obstetrician arrival if any competent operator present.

outcomes.summary: Maternal arrest ≥20 weeks — perimortem CS by 4 min
outcomes.detail: CPR with LUD, no transfer to theatre, hands higher on sternum.

references.label: Resuscitation Council UK Adult Advanced Life Support 2021 — Special Circumstances: Pregnancy

title: Obstetric fistula — recognition and referral
description: Suspect obstetric fistula in any woman with continuous urinary or faecal incontinence after prolonged obstructed labour, particularly in low-resource settings. Catheterise immediately on diagnosis of obstructed labour — early bladder rest may allow small fistulae to heal. Refer to specialist fistula centre (Hamlin Fistula Hospitals, partner sites) for surgical repair after 3 months of healing. Provide skin care, dignity, and counselling; treat depression and stigma.

outcomes.summary: Obstetric fistula — catheterise + specialist surgical referral
outcomes.detail: Early catheter may allow healing; otherwise surgical repair after 3 months.

references.label: WHO 10 facts on obstetric fistula 2018
FIGO Global Competency-Based Fistula Surgery Training Manual 2011

title: Puerperal psychosis — urgent psychiatric admission
description: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency. Onset usually within first 2 weeks postpartum; features include rapid mood swings, mania, hallucinations, delusions, confusion. Risk factors: previous postpartum psychosis (40-50% recurrence), bipolar disorder, family history. Admit to a mother-and-baby unit ideally. Treatment: lithium, antipsychotic (olanzapine, quetiapine), ECT for severe/refractory. Suicide and infanticide risk — do not leave the woman alone with the baby until safe. Pre-pregnancy planning in bipolar — prophylactic lithium peri-delivery may prevent recurrence.

outcomes.summary: Puerperal psychosis — emergency admission to mother-baby unit
outcomes.detail: High suicide/infanticide risk; lithium and atypical antipsychotic; do not leave alone with infant.

references.label: NICE CG192 Antenatal and postnatal mental health 2014 (updated 2020)
MBRRACE-UK Saving Lives, Improving Mothers' Care 2023

title: Safe abortion care — WHO 2022 guideline
description: Provide safe abortion within the limits of national law. Medical abortion up to 12 weeks: mifepristone 200 mg orally, followed by misoprostol 800 mcg buccal/sublingual/vaginal 24-48 hours later (additional doses 4-hourly if needed). Beyond 12 weeks medical: mifepristone + misoprostol 400 mcg every 3 h. Surgical abortion: manual vacuum aspiration up to 12-14 weeks; dilatation and evacuation beyond. Post-abortion contraception offered before discharge (immediate IUD/implant feasible). Anti-D for RhD-negative >12 weeks (and consider 10-12 weeks). Post-abortion care for incomplete abortion uses the same misoprostol regimens.

outcomes.summary: Safe abortion — mifepristone + misoprostol up to 12 weeks medical
outcomes.detail: Immediate contraception offered; anti-D if RhD-negative after 12 weeks.

references.label: WHO Abortion care guideline 2022

codings.display: Encounter for elective termination of pregnancy

title: Antenatal anaemia — screening and treatment
description: Screen Hb at booking and at 28 weeks. Diagnose anaemia: Hb <110 g/L first trimester, <105 g/L second and third trimester, <100 g/L postpartum. First-line: oral iron 100-200 mg elemental daily (ferrous sulfate, fumarate, or gluconate) once daily or alternate-day dosing. IV iron if intolerance, malabsorption, or Hb <105 g/L at 34+ weeks. Transfusion only if Hb <70 g/L with symptoms or significant clinical compromise. Investigate non-iron-deficient anaemia (folate, B12, haemoglobinopathy).

outcomes.summary: Antenatal anaemia — oral iron then IV if poor response
outcomes.detail: Alternate-day dosing may improve tolerability; investigate non-IDA causes.

references.label: BSH UK Guideline on the management of iron deficiency in pregnancy 2020

title: Syphilis in pregnancy — benzathine penicillin G
description: Treat any positive maternal syphilis serology in pregnancy with benzathine penicillin G IM. Early syphilis (primary, secondary, early latent): single 2.4 MU dose, repeated at 1 week in pregnancy. Late latent or unknown duration: 2.4 MU weekly for three doses. Penicillin-allergic women: desensitise and treat with penicillin (no acceptable alternative for pregnancy). Treat partners. Universal antenatal screening at first contact; rescreen at 28-32 weeks in high-prevalence settings.

outcomes.summary: Syphilis in pregnancy — benzathine penicillin G IM weekly
outcomes.detail: No alternative for penicillin allergy — desensitise. Treat partners.

references.label: WHO Guidelines for the Treatment of Treponema pallidum (syphilis) 2016
CDC STI Treatment Guidelines 2021

title: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy — treat
description: Asymptomatic bacteriuria affects 2-10% of pregnant women and untreated raises risk of pyelonephritis, preterm birth, and low birthweight. Screen with MSU culture at booking. Treat any positive culture (≥10⁵ CFU/mL of a single organism). Options: nitrofurantoin 50 mg QDS 7 days (avoid term and G6PD), cefalexin 500 mg TDS 7 days, amoxicillin 500 mg TDS 7 days (if susceptible), pivmecillinam 400 mg TDS 3-7 days. Repeat MSU at 2 weeks post-treatment; persistent — extended course and consider prophylaxis. Treat GBS bacteriuria and offer intrapartum prophylaxis.

outcomes.summary: ASB in pregnancy — treat by sensitivities
outcomes.detail: Avoid nitrofurantoin at term and trimethoprim in 1st trimester; rescreen at 2 weeks.

references.label: NICE NG109 Urinary tract infection (lower): antimicrobial prescribing 2018

codings.display: Unspecified infection of urinary tract in pregnancy

title: Ectopic pregnancy — diagnostic pathway and methotrexate criteria
description: In a woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain or PV bleeding plus positive pregnancy test, exclude ectopic pregnancy. TVUS — look for intrauterine sac at β-hCG ≥1500 IU/L (discriminatory zone). Methotrexate 50 mg/m² IM single dose appropriate for haemodynamically stable, unruptured, mass <35 mm, no fetal heart, β-hCG <5000 IU/L, willing/able to follow up. Surgical management (laparoscopic salpingectomy or salpingotomy) for ruptured, haemodynamically unstable, contraindications to MTX, or patient preference. Expectant management only for very low and falling β-hCG and willing follow-up.

outcomes.summary: Suspected ectopic — TVUS + β-hCG; surgical if unstable/ruptured
outcomes.detail: Methotrexate criteria strict; expectant only for very low and falling β-hCG.

references.label: NICE NG126 Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage 2019 (updated)
RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 21 Tubal Pregnancy 2016

title: Gestational trophoblastic disease — registration and β-hCG follow-up
description: After evacuation of hydatidiform mole, register the woman with a regional gestational trophoblastic disease centre. Serial β-hCG measurements: weekly until normal for 3 consecutive weeks then monthly until 6 months from evacuation (partial mole — 4 weeks after first normal). Avoid pregnancy and use barrier contraception (combined oral contraception acceptable once β-hCG normal). Persistent or rising β-hCG → suspected gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, refer for chemotherapy (single-agent methotrexate for low-risk).

outcomes.summary: GTD — register + β-hCG follow-up; avoid pregnancy during
outcomes.detail: Persistent/rising β-hCG — GTN; chemotherapy referral.

references.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 38 Gestational Trophoblastic Disease 2020

title: Acute aortic dissection — recognition and initial BP control
description: Suspect acute aortic dissection in sudden severe ("tearing") chest or back pain, especially with pulse deficit, BP differential >20 mmHg between arms, new diastolic murmur, neurological deficit, or chest X-ray widened mediastinum. ADD-RS clinical prediction tool with serial D-dimer (negative at <500 ng/mL with low ADD-RS reasonable to exclude). CT angiogram is the definitive investigation. Targets: heart rate 60-80, SBP 100-120 mmHg. Start with esmolol or labetalol IV (beta-blockade first) before vasodilator (nitroprusside, nicardipine) to prevent reflex tachycardia. Stanford A — emergency cardiac surgery; Stanford B — best medical therapy unless complicated.

outcomes.summary: Suspected aortic dissection — beta-block first, then vasodilator; urgent CTA
outcomes.detail: Heart rate first to <80, then SBP 100-120; Stanford A is surgical emergency.

references.label: ESC Guidelines on Aortic Diseases 2024
Rogers AM et al. Sensitivity of the aortic dissection detection risk score. Circulation 2011

title: Pulmonary embolism — sPESI gate to outpatient management
description: For confirmed PE assess severity with simplified PESI (sPESI): age >80, history of cancer, chronic cardiopulmonary disease, HR ≥110, SBP <100, SaO2 <90% — each scores 1 point. sPESI = 0: low risk (30-day mortality ~1%), consider outpatient management with apixaban or rivaroxaban, with safety net and clinical follow-up at 24-72 h. sPESI ≥1: admit. Assess RV strain on echo or CT, troponin, NT-proBNP. Intermediate-high risk PE — consider half-dose thrombolysis or catheter-directed therapy. Massive PE with cardiac arrest or shock — systemic alteplase 50-100 mg.

outcomes.summary: PE — sPESI to guide outpatient vs admission
outcomes.detail: sPESI 0 + no haemodynamic compromise — consider outpatient DOAC.

references.label: ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of acute pulmonary embolism 2019
Jiménez D et al. Simplified PESI. Arch Intern Med 2010

codings.display: Other pulmonary embolism without cor pulmonale

title: Atrial fibrillation — rate vs rhythm control decision
description: Rate control with beta-blocker or rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker (diltiazem/verapamil) is first-line for most. Rhythm control (DC cardioversion or antiarrhythmics or ablation) is preferred if: new onset within 12 months (EAST-AFNET 4 — early rhythm control reduces CV outcomes), heart failure with reduced LVEF (CASTLE-AF — ablation), symptomatic despite rate control, reversible cause, or younger patient. AAD options: flecainide/propafenone in structurally normal heart, amiodarone for HF/structural disease, dronedarone in non-permanent AF without HF.

outcomes.summary: AF — rate-control default; rhythm control if recent onset or HF
outcomes.detail: EAST-AFNET 4 supports rhythm control within 12 months of diagnosis.

references.label: ESC Guidelines for the management of atrial fibrillation 2024
Kirchhof P et al. EAST-AFNET 4. NEJM 2020

title: AF stroke prevention — CHA2DS2-VASc with DOAC selection
description: In AF use CHA2DS2-VASc; offer oral anticoagulation if ≥2 in men or ≥3 in women; consider if ≥1 in men or ≥2 in women. Use HAS-BLED only to identify modifiable bleed risks — not to withhold OAC. DOAC (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, edoxaban) preferred over warfarin (except moderate-severe mitral stenosis, mechanical valves, antiphospholipid syndrome — warfarin only). Apixaban 5 mg BD (2.5 mg BD if ≥2 of: age ≥80, weight ≤60 kg, creatinine ≥133 µmol/L). Renal dosing per drug-specific cutoffs; avoid all DOACs at eGFR <15 (apixaban with caution per local).

outcomes.summary: AF — DOAC by CHA2DS2-VASc; warfarin only for select indications
outcomes.detail: HAS-BLED does not withhold OAC; treat modifiable bleed risks.

references.label: ESC Guidelines for the management of atrial fibrillation 2024
NICE NG196 Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management 2021

title: Acute pericarditis — 4-criteria diagnosis and treatment
description: Diagnose acute pericarditis with ≥2 of: typical pleuritic/positional chest pain (sharp, relieved by sitting forward), pericardial friction rub, new widespread ST elevation or PR depression on ECG, pericardial effusion on echo. Treat with NSAID (ibuprofen 600 mg TDS for 1-2 weeks) plus colchicine 0.5 mg BD (weight ≥70 kg) or 0.5 mg OD (<70 kg) for 3 months — colchicine reduces recurrence by ~50% (COPE/ICAP/CORP). Avoid steroids first-line unless contraindication to NSAID or autoimmune cause. Echocardiogram for tamponade (Beck's triad: hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds) — pericardiocentesis.

outcomes.summary: Acute pericarditis — NSAID + colchicine 3 months
outcomes.detail: Echo for tamponade; avoid steroids first-line.

references.label: ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of pericardial diseases 2015
Imazio M et al. ICAP Trial. NEJM 2013

title: Hypertensive emergency — end-organ damage triage
description: Distinguish hypertensive emergency (severe BP plus acute end-organ damage: hypertensive encephalopathy, ACS, acute LV failure with pulmonary oedema, dissection, AKI/oliguria, stroke, eclampsia, retinal haemorrhage/papilloedema) from urgency (severe BP without end-organ damage). Emergency — IV agent in HDU/ICU, reduce MAP by 25% within 1 hour (slower in stroke). Urgency — oral agents over days; avoid sublingual nifedipine. Agent choice by indication: labetalol (most), nicardipine (LV preserved), GTN (LV failure, ACS), esmolol/labetalol then vasodilator (dissection), labetalol or nicardipine (stroke per BP thresholds), magnesium + labetalol (eclampsia).

outcomes.summary: HTN emergency — IV agent, 25% MAP reduction in 1 h
outcomes.detail: No sublingual nifedipine; agent matched to end-organ involvement.

references.label: ESC Guidelines for the management of arterial hypertension 2023

title: Chest pain — HEART score for ED discharge decision
description: In ED chest pain calculate HEART (History, ECG, Age, Risk factors, Troponin), 0-2 each, total 0-10. Score 0-3 with two negative serial high-sensitivity troponins (0 h and ≥1 or 3 h) — low risk (<2% MACE 30 d), discharge with rapid outpatient follow-up. 4-6 — observation, further investigation. ≥7 — admit, cardiology, consider early invasive strategy. Combine with high-sensitivity troponin pathway (NICE NG185) for accelerated rule-out/rule-in.

outcomes.summary: HEART ≤3 + two negative troponins — safe ED discharge
outcomes.detail: Combine with hs-troponin pathway; outpatient follow-up within 72 h.

references.label: Mahler SA et al. HEART Pathway. Circ Cardiovasc Qual Outcomes 2015
NICE NG185 Acute coronary syndromes 2020

title: STEMI — fibrinolysis criteria and tenecteplase weight-banded dose
description: Offer fibrinolysis for STEMI when primary PCI cannot be delivered within 120 min of diagnosis, symptom onset within 12 hours (consider up to 24 h if ongoing pain/instability). Tenecteplase IV bolus by weight: <60 kg 30 mg; 60-69 kg 35 mg; 70-79 kg 40 mg; 80-89 kg 45 mg; ≥90 kg 50 mg. Half-dose for age ≥75 years. Concurrent enoxaparin (30 mg IV + 1 mg/kg SC, max 100 mg first two doses) and clopidogrel 300 mg (75 mg if ≥75 years) loading. Transfer to PCI centre after fibrinolysis (pharmaco-invasive strategy). Absolute contraindications include prior ICH, ischaemic stroke <6 months, CNS neoplasm, major trauma/surgery <3 weeks, active bleeding, aortic dissection.

outcomes.summary: STEMI — fibrinolysis if PCI delay >120 min; tenecteplase weight-banded
outcomes.detail: Half-dose tenecteplase if ≥75 y; transfer to PCI centre after lysis.

references.label: ESC Guidelines for the management of acute coronary syndromes 2023

title: STEMI — primary PCI within 120 min first medical contact to balloon
description: For STEMI primary PCI is preferred reperfusion when achievable within 120 minutes of first medical contact (target ≤90 min for direct presentation). Activate cath lab in parallel with ED workup. Pre-PCI: aspirin 300 mg loading + P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor 180 mg or prasugrel 60 mg unless contraindicated — bleed risk, low body weight, prior stroke for prasugrel), anticoagulation (UFH/bivalirudin per local protocol). Cardiogenic shock — IABP no routine benefit; consider mechanical support (Impella, ECMO) per local algorithm.

outcomes.summary: STEMI — primary PCI within 120 min of FMC
outcomes.detail: Aspirin + P2Y12 + anticoagulation; activate cath lab in parallel with ED workup.

references.label: ESC Guidelines for the management of acute coronary syndromes 2023

title: Acute kidney injury — KDIGO bundle
description: KDIGO AKI definition: rise in creatinine ≥26 µmol/L within 48 h, or ≥1.5× baseline within 7 days, or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 h. Bundle: review fluid status (hypovolaemia, overload), STOP nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, ACEi/ARBs, gentamicin, contrast), urinalysis and urine PCR, US renal tract within 24 h if obstruction suspected or cause unclear, daily creatinine and electrolytes, refer nephrology if stage 3 (creatinine ≥3× baseline or ≥354 µmol/L) or need for RRT.

outcomes.summary: AKI — KDIGO bundle: fluids, stop nephrotoxics, US, electrolytes
outcomes.detail: Refer nephrology if stage 3 or unclear cause; daily monitoring.

references.label: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury 2012

title: ARDS — Berlin criteria and lung-protective ventilation
description: Berlin criteria: acute onset within 1 week, bilateral opacities on chest imaging not explained by effusion/atelectasis/nodules, respiratory failure not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload, PaO2/FiO2 ratio with PEEP ≥5 cmH2O: mild 200-300, moderate 100-200, severe ≤100. Lung-protective ventilation: tidal volume 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, plateau pressure ≤30 cmH2O, driving pressure ≤15 cmH2O, PEEP per FiO2 table (ARDSNet/LOV), proning ≥16 hours/day for severe ARDS (PROSEVA), neuromuscular blockade selectively. Conservative fluid strategy; ECMO referral if refractory.

outcomes.summary: ARDS — lung-protective ventilation (6 mL/kg PBW) + prone if severe
outcomes.detail: Plateau ≤30, driving pressure ≤15; prone ≥16 h/day for P/F <150.

references.label: ATS/ESICM/SCCM Clinical Practice Guideline: Mechanical Ventilation in ARDS 2017
PROSEVA NEJM 2013

title: Massive haemorrhage — activation triggers and 1:1:1 ratios
description: Activate massive haemorrhage protocol when: ABC score ≥2 (penetrating mechanism, SBP <90, HR >120, positive FAST), shock index >0.9 with active bleeding, expected need for ≥4 RBC units in 1 hour, or rapid clinical deterioration. Use 1:1:1 ratio of RBC : FFP : platelets (PROPPR) or 1:1:0.5 per local. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours (CRASH-2/CRASH-3/MATTERs). Calcium for citrate-related hypocalcaemia. Permissive hypotension (SBP 80-90) in penetrating trauma without head injury until source controlled. Damage-control surgery and angio-embolisation.

outcomes.summary: Massive haemorrhage — activate MHP, 1:1:1, TXA within 3 h
outcomes.detail: Permissive hypotension in penetrating trauma without head injury; correct calcium.

references.label: PROPPR Trial JAMA 2015
CRASH-2 Lancet 2010

title: Trauma laparotomy — absolute and relative indications
description: Absolute indications for trauma laparotomy: penetrating abdominal injury with peritonism/evisceration/haemodynamic instability/free air on imaging, blunt abdominal trauma with peritonism, positive FAST in unstable patient, gastrointestinal bleeding from penetrating injury. Relative: positive DPL >100 000 RBC/mm³, persistent unexplained hypotension. Selective non-operative management for stable blunt solid-organ injury with CT-graded haemorrhage and ongoing observation; angio-embolisation as adjunct. Damage-control laparotomy for unstable patient — stop bleeding, control contamination, abbreviated closure, return to ICU.

outcomes.summary: Trauma — peritonism/instability/penetrating = laparotomy
outcomes.detail: Stable blunt solid organ may be managed selectively non-operatively with imaging follow-up.

references.label: EAST Practice Management Guidelines for Selective Nonoperative Management of Penetrating Abdominal Trauma 2010

title: Carbon monoxide poisoning — HBOT criteria
description: Carboxyhaemoglobin >15-20% or any symptom — high-flow 100% oxygen via non-rebreather. Consider hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) for: loss of consciousness at any time, neurological signs/seizures/coma, COHb >25% (>20% in pregnancy), cardiac ischaemia or arrhythmia, pregnant with COHb >15% (fetal CO half-life longer than maternal), persistent symptoms after 4-6 h of normobaric O2. Treat for 6-12 h with normobaric O2 even if no HBOT available. Long-term — counsel about delayed neuropsychiatric sequelae and arrange follow-up.

outcomes.summary: CO poisoning — 100% O2 + HBOT if LOC, neuro, pregnant, COHb>25%
outcomes.detail: COHb does not correlate well with severity — clinical features drive HBOT decision.

references.label: Undersea and Hyperbaric Medical Society indications for HBOT 2023

codings.display: Toxic effect of carbon monoxide, undetermined

title: Exertional heat stroke — cool first, transport second
description: Exertional heat stroke = core temperature >40°C with CNS dysfunction (confusion, ataxia, seizure, coma). Cool the patient BEFORE transport. Cold water immersion (ice bath, 1-15°C) is the fastest method — survival approaches 100% if cooling started within 30 min. Alternatives: tarp-assisted cooling, fans + cold water spray, ice-packs to neck/axilla/groin. Stop cooling at core 38.5-39°C to avoid overshoot. Treat seizures with benzodiazepines; rhabdomyolysis common — fluid and urine output monitoring; check coagulation for heat-related DIC.

outcomes.summary: Exertional heat stroke — cool first via CWI before transport
outcomes.detail: Aim cooling rate ≥0.15°C/min; stop at 38.5-39°C.

references.label: Wilderness Medical Society Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Heat Illness 2024 update

title: Hyponatraemia — severity-banded correction with ODS prevention
description: Severe symptomatic (seizures, GCS <8, coma): 150 mL 3% hypertonic saline IV over 10-20 minutes, repeat × 2 if no improvement, target rise 4-6 mmol/L in first hour then stop. Moderate symptomatic (vomiting, confusion): 100-150 mL 3% saline over 20-30 min. Asymptomatic chronic: identify cause, fluid restriction (SIADH), saline (hypovolaemia), no aggressive correction. CORRECTION LIMIT: ≤10 mmol/L in any 24 h period and ≤18 mmol/L in 48 h — exceeding risks osmotic demyelination syndrome (especially malnourished, alcohol, liver disease, severe hypokalaemia). If overcorrection occurs give 5% dextrose ± desmopressin to bring level down.

outcomes.summary: Hyponatraemia — limit correction ≤10 mmol/L/24 h to avoid ODS
outcomes.detail: Severe symptomatic — 3% saline boluses; overcorrection — dextrose + desmopressin rescue.

references.label: European Society of Endocrinology Clinical practice guideline on diagnosis and treatment of hyponatraemia 2014

title: Hyperkalaemia — emergency bundle
description: K >6.0 mmol/L or ECG changes (peaked T, wide QRS, sine wave) — bundle: (1) calcium gluconate 10% 10-20 mL IV over 5-10 min to stabilise myocardium (repeat in 5 min if ECG unchanged); (2) insulin 10 units in 50 mL 50% dextrose IV over 15-30 min (monitor glucose 1-hourly for 6 h — risk of late hypoglycaemia); (3) salbutamol 10-20 mg nebulised (caution in ischaemic heart disease); (4) sodium bicarbonate 50 mmol IV only if metabolic acidosis (pH <7.2); (5) elimination — calcium resonium / patiromer / sodium zirconium cyclosilicate; (6) dialysis if refractory or AKI/anuria. Stop ACEi/ARB/MRA/NSAIDs.

outcomes.summary: Hyperkalaemia — calcium + insulin-dextrose + salbutamol + remove K
outcomes.detail: Calcium first if ECG changes; dialysis if refractory or AKI.

references.label: UK Renal Association Clinical Practice Guidelines: Treatment of Acute Hyperkalaemia in Adults 2023

title: Hypocalcaemia — IV calcium for acute, oral for chronic
description: Symptomatic or severe (corrected Ca <1.9 mmol/L or any seizure, tetany, prolonged QT): 10% calcium gluconate 10-20 mL IV over 10 min, then infusion of 10 vials in 1 L saline at 50-100 mL/h, titrate. Avoid calcium chloride peripherally — extravasation necroses. Correct magnesium concurrently (often coexists). Asymptomatic mild-moderate: oral calcium carbonate 500-1000 mg elemental TDS with meals, plus vitamin D (cholecalciferol 800-2000 IU/day or alfacalcidol 0.5-1 mcg/day in hypoparathyroidism). Identify cause: hypoparathyroidism (post-thyroidectomy), CKD, vitamin D deficiency, pancreatitis, sepsis, tumour lysis.

outcomes.summary: Hypocalcaemia — IV gluconate if symptomatic; treat Mg concurrently
outcomes.detail: Avoid CaCl peripherally; oral with vit D for chronic.

references.label: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Treatment of Hypoparathyroidism 2016

title: Thyroid storm — Burch-Wartofsky scoring and treatment
description: Burch-Wartofsky Point Scale assesses thermoregulatory, CNS, GI/hepatic, cardiovascular, congestive heart failure dysfunction and precipitant — score ≥45 highly suggestive of storm, 25-44 impending storm. Treatment: propylthiouracil 200-400 mg every 4-6 h (preferred over methimazole in storm due to peripheral T4→T3 block) ORALLY/NG; iodine (Lugol's 8 drops every 6 h or potassium iodide), starting AT LEAST 1 hour AFTER PTU/MMI; hydrocortisone 100 mg IV every 8 h (suppresses T4→T3 and treats adrenal insufficiency); beta-blocker (propranolol 60-80 mg every 4-6 h or esmolol infusion if HF). Cooling, IV fluids, treat precipitant (infection, DKA, surgery, trauma), HDU.

outcomes.summary: Thyroid storm — PTU first, then iodine, plus hydrocortisone + beta-blocker
outcomes.detail: Burch-Wartofsky ≥45 — full storm; PTU before iodine to block organification.

references.label: ATA Guidelines for Diagnosis and Management of Hyperthyroidism 2016

codings.display: Thyrotoxicosis with thyrotoxic crisis or storm

title: Adrenal crisis — hydrocortisone 100 mg IV stat
description: Suspect adrenal crisis in known/at-risk adrenal insufficiency with hypotension, vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion, fever, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia and/or hyperkalaemia, especially during infection/illness/surgery. Treat empirically — do NOT wait for confirmation. Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV/IM stat, then 200 mg/24 h continuous infusion or 50 mg IV every 6 h. IV crystalloid 1 L in first hour. Treat precipitant. Patient education and steroid emergency card; train patient/family in IM hydrocortisone for emergencies; double sick-day dosing.

outcomes.summary: Adrenal crisis — hydrocortisone 100 mg IV without delay
outcomes.detail: Continue 200 mg/24 h infusion; IV fluids; treat precipitant; provide emergency card and IM kit.

references.label: Society for Endocrinology Emergency Management of Acute Adrenal Insufficiency 2016

title: Pituitary apoplexy — steroids and neurosurgical referral
description: Sudden headache, visual disturbance (especially bitemporal hemianopia or cranial nerve palsy III/IV/VI), reduced consciousness, signs of acute pituitary insufficiency. MRI pituitary urgent (haemorrhage/infarction in adenoma). Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV stat then 200 mg/24 h or 50 mg every 6 h — do not delay for biochemistry. Refer urgently to endocrinology and neurosurgery; transsphenoidal decompression considered for visual deterioration. Replace anterior pituitary hormones as needed; permanent hypopituitarism common.

outcomes.summary: Pituitary apoplexy — hydrocortisone + neurosurgery referral
outcomes.detail: Urgent MRI; do not delay steroids; visual deterioration may need surgical decompression.

references.label: UK guidelines for the management of pituitary apoplexy 2011

title: Acute mesenteric ischaemia — lactate, CT angiography, urgent revascularisation
description: Suspect AMI in disproportionate abdominal pain with relatively unremarkable examination, raised lactate, AF or vascular disease. CT angiography is first-line imaging. Resuscitate, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, anticoagulate with UFH unless contraindicated. Urgent vascular surgery and interventional radiology: embolectomy or stent for embolic/thrombotic SMA; resect non-viable bowel; second-look laparotomy at 24-48 h. Non-occlusive (NOMI) — treat underlying low cardiac output, vasodilator infusion. Venous mesenteric thrombosis — anticoagulation, supportive.

outcomes.summary: Acute mesenteric ischaemia — CT angio + urgent vascular/IR
outcomes.detail: Pain out of proportion + raised lactate + AF/vascular risk = AMI until disproven.

references.label: European Society for Vascular Surgery Guidelines on the Management of Mesenteric Ischaemia 2017

title: Tumour lysis syndrome — prevention and treatment
description: Risk stratify before cytotoxic chemotherapy or targeted therapy. High risk (high WBC haematological malignancies, bulky lymphoma, certain solid tumours): IV hydration 2-3 L/m²/day, allopurinol 300 mg/day OR rasburicase 0.2 mg/kg/day for 1-5 days if very high risk or G6PD-tested negative. Monitor potassium, phosphate, urate, calcium, creatinine, LDH every 6-8 h for 24-48 h. Established TLS: aggressive IV hydration, rasburicase, treat hyperkalaemia/hyperphosphataemia/hypocalcaemia, RRT if oliguric or refractory electrolyte derangement. Avoid calcium repletion unless symptomatic (precipitates calcium phosphate in tissue).

outcomes.summary: TLS — risk-stratify, hydrate, allopurinol/rasburicase, RRT if refractory
outcomes.detail: Avoid calcium replacement unless symptomatic — risk of metastatic calcification.

references.label: British Committee for Standards in Haematology Guidelines for the management of tumour lysis syndrome 2015

title: Sepsis — Surviving Sepsis 1-hour bundle
description: For suspected sepsis with hypoperfusion or septic shock, within 1 hour: measure lactate (remeasure if >2 mmol/L), obtain blood cultures BEFORE antibiotics where possible without delay, administer broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 h, begin 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid for hypotension or lactate >4 mmol/L (slower in HF/cirrhosis), start vasopressor (noradrenaline first-line) for persistent MAP <65 after fluid. Reassess perfusion frequently. Source control within 6-12 hours when feasible (drainage, debridement, device removal).

outcomes.summary: Sepsis 1-h bundle — lactate, cultures, antibiotics, fluids, vasopressor
outcomes.detail: Noradrenaline first-line vasopressor; source control within 6-12 h.

references.label: Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines for the Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2021

title: Septic shock — vasopressor and inotrope selection
description: First-line vasopressor: noradrenaline (norepinephrine) titrated to MAP ≥65 mmHg. Add vasopressin 0.03 U/min if noradrenaline dose escalating (e.g. >0.25 mcg/kg/min) to spare noradrenaline. Adrenaline (epinephrine) third-line or alternative. Dopamine is NOT first-line for septic shock (excess arrhythmia). Add dobutamine or low-dose adrenaline if cardiac dysfunction with hypoperfusion despite adequate MAP. Hydrocortisone 200 mg/24 h IV for refractory shock requiring noradrenaline ≥0.25 mcg/kg/min for ≥4 h.

outcomes.summary: Septic shock — noradrenaline first; add vasopressin then hydrocortisone
outcomes.detail: Dopamine not first-line; dobutamine for cardiac dysfunction; HC for catecholamine-resistant.

references.label: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021

title: Community-acquired pneumonia — severity assessment with ICU minor criteria
description: Use CURB-65 (Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L, RR ≥30, BP SBP<90 or DBP≤60, age ≥65) for outpatient/inpatient decision. Score 0-1 — outpatient, 2 — short stay or inpatient, ≥3 — inpatient and consider ICU. ATS/IDSA minor criteria for ICU admission (≥3 of: RR ≥30, P/F ≤250, multilobar, confusion, uraemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, hypothermia, hypotension requiring fluids); or major: septic shock requiring vasopressors, mechanical ventilation. Add macrolide or fluoroquinolone for atypical cover. Influenza testing in season; oseltamivir within 48 h.

outcomes.summary: Severe CAP — CURB-65 + ATS/IDSA minor criteria for ICU
outcomes.detail: Atypical cover; consider influenza antiviral in season.

references.label: ATS/IDSA Clinical Practice Guideline for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Adults with Community-acquired Pneumonia 2019

title: Acute liver failure — King's College Criteria for transplant referral
description: Acute liver failure: jaundice + coagulopathy (INR ≥1.5) + altered mental status in a patient without prior liver disease, illness <26 weeks. Refer to liver transplant centre for early evaluation. King's Criteria — paracetamol: arterial pH <7.30, OR all of (creatinine >300 µmol/L, INR >6.5, grade 3-4 encephalopathy), OR lactate >3.5 mmol/L after 4 h fluid resuscitation. Non-paracetamol: INR >6.5, OR any 3 of: age <10 or >40, drug/halothane/non-A non-B/non-E aetiology, jaundice >7 days before encephalopathy, INR >3.5, bilirubin >300 µmol/L. N-acetylcysteine for paracetamol and non-paracetamol non-hyperacute. ICU; hyperammonaemia (>150) — renal replacement.

outcomes.summary: Acute liver failure — early transplant centre referral; King's Criteria
outcomes.detail: NAC for paracetamol and non-paracetamol non-hyperacute; ICU support; ammonia → RRT.

references.label: AASLD Practice Guideline on the management of acute liver failure 2011 (with updates)

title: Acute pancreatitis — severity stratification (Atlanta 2012)
description: Diagnose with 2 of 3: typical abdominal pain, lipase/amylase ≥3× ULN, characteristic imaging. Stratify severity using Revised Atlanta Criteria — Mild (no organ failure, no complications), Moderate (transient organ failure <48 h or local complications), Severe (persistent organ failure >48 h). Bedside tools: BISAP (BUN >25, impaired mental status, SIRS, age >60, pleural effusion — each 1 point, ≥3 high mortality), HAPS for low risk. Fluid resuscitation with balanced crystalloid (Ringer's or Hartmann's) 5-10 mL/kg/h titrated to UO and lactate (avoid 0.9% saline). Early enteral feeding within 24-72 h. Antibiotics ONLY for proven infected necrosis. ERCP urgent (<24 h) for cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction.

outcomes.summary: Acute pancreatitis — Atlanta severity + balanced crystalloid + early enteral feed
outcomes.detail: No prophylactic antibiotics; ERCP <24 h only for cholangitis or persistent obstruction.

references.label: AGA Clinical Practice Update on Management of Acute Pancreatitis 2021
IAP/APA evidence-based guidelines 2013

title: Deep vein thrombosis — Wells + D-dimer pathway
description: Use the two-level DVT Wells score. Likely (≥2 points) — proximal-leg US within 4 hours (if not possible, interim DOAC and US within 24 h). Unlikely (<2 points) — D-dimer; negative excludes DVT, positive proceed to US. Treat confirmed proximal DVT with DOAC (apixaban or rivaroxaban first-line) at induction doses (apixaban 10 mg BD × 7 days then 5 mg BD; rivaroxaban 15 mg BD × 21 days then 20 mg OD). Duration 3 months provoked, ≥3 months unprovoked (consider extended). Cancer-associated thrombosis — DOAC or LMWH per malignancy.

outcomes.summary: Suspected DVT — Wells + D-dimer + US pathway
outcomes.detail: Apixaban/rivaroxaban first-line; cancer-associated — DOAC or LMWH.

references.label: NICE NG158 Venous thromboembolic diseases: diagnosis, management and thrombophilia testing 2020

codings.display: Acute embolism and thrombosis of unspecified deep veins of lower extremity

title: Ischaemic stroke — IV thrombolysis criteria and time window
description: Offer IV alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg, 10% bolus, rest over 1 h) for acute ischaemic stroke within 4.5 hours of symptom onset (or last known well), when CT excludes haemorrhage. Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg single bolus IV being adopted as alternative. Extended window (4.5-9 h) with perfusion-CT/MRI mismatch (target mismatch ratio per EXTEND/WAKE-UP). BP control to <185/110 before lysis. Exclusions: SBP >185 despite treatment, INR >1.7/active anticoagulant, recent major surgery/trauma, GI bleed <21 d, prior ICH, large infarct on imaging. Mechanical thrombectomy for LVO up to 24 h with perfusion-imaging selection (DAWN/DEFUSE-3).

outcomes.summary: Acute ischaemic stroke <4.5 h — IV alteplase if no contraindication
outcomes.detail: Tenecteplase increasingly used; LVO — thrombectomy up to 24 h with imaging selection.

references.label: AHA/ASA Guidelines for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke 2019 (updated)

title: Acute ICH — rapid BP control to SBP ~140 mmHg
description: In spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage with SBP 150-220 mmHg, aim for SBP ~140 mmHg using IV labetalol or nicardipine within 1 hour, maintained 24 hours. INTERACT-3 supports a bundle of intensive BP control, glycaemic control, fever management, and reversal of anticoagulation. Reverse anticoagulant: vitamin K + PCC for warfarin (INR target <1.3 within 4 h); idarucizumab for dabigatran; andexanet alfa or PCC for FXa inhibitors; tranexamic acid considered but not standard. Surgical evacuation for cerebellar haemorrhage ≥3 cm or causing brainstem compression; selected supratentorial cases.

outcomes.summary: Spontaneous ICH — SBP to ~140 mmHg + reverse anticoagulant
outcomes.detail: INTERACT-3 bundle; cerebellar haemorrhage ≥3 cm — surgical evacuation.

references.label: INTERACT-3 Lancet 2023
AHA/ASA Guideline for the Management of Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage 2022

title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage — recognition and Ottawa SAH rule
description: Sudden thunderclap headache, peaking within 1 min, exclude SAH. Ottawa SAH Rule (alert ≥15 y, new severe non-traumatic headache, peaking within 1 hour): age ≥40, neck pain or stiffness, witnessed LOC, onset during exertion, thunderclap (instant peak), neck flexion limitation. If any present — image (non-contrast CT within 6 h has 99% sensitivity; if >6 h or negative — LP for xanthochromia at ≥12 h post onset, or CT angiography). Refer all confirmed SAH to neurosurgery; nimodipine 60 mg every 4 h for 21 days to reduce vasospasm; control BP <160 mmHg until aneurysm secured.

outcomes.summary: Thunderclap headache — Ottawa SAH rule → CT/LP
outcomes.detail: CT <6 h excludes most; nimodipine 60 mg q4h × 21 d; neurosurgical referral.

references.label: Perry JJ et al. Ottawa subarachnoid haemorrhage rule. JAMA 2013
NICE NG228 Stroke and transient ischaemic attack 2022

title: Cardiogenic shock — initial management and mechanical support triggers
description: Recognise cardiogenic shock by SBP <90 mmHg or need for vasopressors with signs of hypoperfusion (cold extremities, oliguria, altered mental status, raised lactate) and cardiac dysfunction (low CI, raised PCWP). Initial: noradrenaline preferred over dopamine (lower mortality, SOAP-II), add dobutamine for low CI. Treat cause — revascularise AMI (CULPRIT-SHOCK: PCI culprit only), arrhythmia, valve disease, tamponade. Mechanical support escalation: IABP (no routine benefit), Impella (selected), VA-ECMO for refractory; bridge to recovery or transplant in shock teams.

outcomes.summary: Cardiogenic shock — noradrenaline + dobutamine; revascularise AMI cause
outcomes.detail: IABP not routinely beneficial; ECMO/Impella in shock-team pathways.

references.label: Thiele H et al. CULPRIT-SHOCK. NEJM 2017
ESC ACS Guidelines 2023

title: Adult anaphylaxis — IM adrenaline 500 mcg in mid-thigh
description: Adult anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (500 mcg) into anterolateral mid-thigh, repeat every 5 min if no improvement. Lay flat, legs elevated (left lateral in pregnancy); high-flow oxygen; IV crystalloid bolus 500-1000 mL if hypotensive; second-line IV hydrocortisone 200 mg, chlorphenamine 10 mg only after stabilisation (not first-line). Refractory anaphylaxis (>2 IM doses): start adrenaline infusion 0.1-1 mcg/kg/min in HDU/ICU. Observe ≥6-12 h depending on severity. Discharge with two adrenaline auto-injectors, written action plan, and allergy clinic referral.

outcomes.summary: Adult anaphylaxis — IM adrenaline 0.5 mg mid-thigh, repeat at 5 min
outcomes.detail: Steroids and antihistamines secondary; refractory — adrenaline infusion; observe 6-12 h.

references.label: Resuscitation Council UK Emergency Treatment of Anaphylaxis 2021

title: Paracetamol overdose — N-acetylcysteine using Rumack-Matthew
description: Take a paracetamol level at 4 hours post-ingestion (single overdose). Plot on Rumack-Matthew nomogram (UK 100-line treatment line, unified across risk groups since 2012). Start NAC if level above the line, or staggered/unknown timing with >75 mg/kg (or unable to assess). 21-h IV NAC: 150 mg/kg over 1 h, then 50 mg/kg over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg over 16 h. SNAP regimen (300 mg/kg over 12 h) being adopted. Continue NAC beyond standard course if INR >1.3, ALT rising, or ongoing toxicity. Refer to liver unit if King's Criteria met or lactate >3 after 4 h fluids.

outcomes.summary: Paracetamol overdose — Rumack-Matthew + NAC; refer liver if severe
outcomes.detail: Single line above 100 mg/L at 4 h is the UK treatment threshold; staggered/unknown — treat without delay.

references.label: MHRA Updated overdose advice for paracetamol 2012
TOXBASE paracetamol overdose monograph

title: Opioid overdose — naloxone titration
description: Suspect opioid toxicity by classic triad: respiratory depression (RR <12 or apnoea), miosis (may be absent in mixed overdose or hypoxia), and decreased consciousness. Give naloxone 400 mcg IM or 100-200 mcg IV titrated to respiratory rate (aim RR ≥12), repeated every 2-3 min. Long-acting opioids (methadone, sustained-release morphine) — naloxone infusion (start at 60% of effective bolus per hour). Do NOT aim to wake the patient — risk of acute withdrawal. Observe ≥6 h after last naloxone (longer for long-acting opioids/methadone). Refer to substance use service; offer take-home naloxone kit and harm-reduction advice.

outcomes.summary: Opioid overdose — naloxone titrated to respiration
outcomes.detail: Goal RR ≥12, not full alertness; infusion for long-acting opioids; observe 6 h minimum.

references.label: WHO Community management of opioid overdose 2014

title: TCA overdose — sodium bicarbonate for QRS >100 ms
description: Suspect TCA toxicity with anticholinergic features, hypotension, seizures and ECG changes. ECG: QRS >100 ms, R wave in aVR >3 mm, R/S ratio aVR >0.7 predict serious toxicity. Treatment: secure airway, lavage if <1 h post ingestion and not contraindicated; sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg IV bolus for QRS >100 ms, ventricular arrhythmia, or hypotension, then infusion to keep arterial pH 7.45-7.55. Avoid Class IA/IC antiarrhythmics and physostigmine. Lipid emulsion as rescue for refractory cardiotoxicity. ICU admission; benzodiazepines for seizures.

outcomes.summary: TCA overdose — sodium bicarbonate for QRS >100 ms
outcomes.detail: Avoid Class IA/IC; lipid emulsion as rescue; benzodiazepines for seizures.

references.label: TOXBASE Tricyclic antidepressant overdose monograph

title: Salicylate poisoning — alkalinisation and dialysis criteria
description: Suspect aspirin toxicity with tinnitus, hyperventilation (respiratory alkalosis), nausea, sweating; later metabolic acidosis with anion gap, hyperthermia, altered consciousness. Plasma salicylate at 4 h and 2-4-hourly until peak. Urinary alkalinisation: sodium bicarbonate 1.5 L 1.26% or 225 mmol over 4 h to target urinary pH 7.5-8.5; monitor potassium (hypokalaemia prevents alkaline urine). Haemodialysis indications: level >700 mg/L (>5 mmol/L) acute or >500 mg/L with severe acidosis/CNS features, renal failure, refractory hyperthermia, pulmonary oedema. NEVER intubate without dialysis ready — apnoea worsens acidaemia.

outcomes.summary: Salicylate poisoning — alkalinise urine; HD for severe
outcomes.detail: Do not intubate without dialysis ready — apnoea precipitates acidosis and arrest.

references.label: TOXBASE Salicylate poisoning monograph

title: Organophosphate poisoning — atropine and pralidoxime
description: Cholinergic toxidrome (SLUDGE/DUMBELS): salivation, lacrimation, urination, defaecation, GI cramps, emesis; miosis, bradycardia, bronchorrhoea, bronchoconstriction, fasciculations, weakness. Secure airway; remove contaminated clothing; PPE for staff. Atropine 2-5 mg IV, double every 5 minutes until secretions dry and BP/HR adequate; continue infusion. Pralidoxime 30 mg/kg IV over 30 min then 8-10 mg/kg/h within first 24-48 h. Diazepam for seizures and to prevent CNS damage. ICU monitoring for intermediate syndrome days 1-4. Differentiate from carbamate (shorter-lived; pralidoxime less critical).

outcomes.summary: Organophosphate poisoning — atropine titrated + pralidoxime + PPE
outcomes.detail: Double atropine until secretions dry; pralidoxime in first 24-48 h; ICU.

references.label: WHO Pesticide poisoning practical guide 2008

codings.display: Toxic effect of organophosphate and carbamate insecticides

title: Methaemoglobinaemia — methylene blue criteria
description: Suspect methaemoglobinaemia in cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen, chocolate-brown blood, normal PaO2 with low SaO2 (pulse oximetry inaccurate). Co-oximetry confirms. Treat with methylthioninium chloride (methylene blue) 1-2 mg/kg IV over 5 min if MetHb >25% (or >15% with symptoms), repeat at 30-60 min if needed. CONTRAINDICATED in G6PD deficiency — can cause acute haemolysis; alternative is ascorbic acid IV high-dose or exchange transfusion. Identify cause: dapsone, sulfonamides, benzocaine, nitrites, aniline dyes; remove exposure.

outcomes.summary: Methaemoglobinaemia — methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg IV; CI in G6PD
outcomes.detail: Ascorbic acid or exchange transfusion in G6PD; remove offending agent.

references.label: TOXBASE Methaemoglobinaemia monograph

title: Cyanide poisoning — hydroxocobalamin first-line
description: Suspect cyanide in smoke inhalation (fire victims), industrial exposure, or unexplained metabolic acidosis with high anion gap and high lactate (>10 mmol/L) and normal-to-high venous SaO2. Hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV over 15 min (paediatric 70 mg/kg, max 5 g) — first-line and safe before lab confirmation. Sodium thiosulfate 12.5 g IV is adjunct. Sodium nitrite (induces methaemoglobinaemia) — only if hydroxocobalamin unavailable AND not in smoke inhalation (methaemoglobinaemia compounds hypoxia). High-flow oxygen, supportive care.

outcomes.summary: Suspected cyanide — hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV first-line
outcomes.detail: Avoid sodium nitrite in smoke inhalation; sodium thiosulfate as adjunct.

references.label: TOXBASE Cyanide poisoning monograph

title: Iron poisoning — deferoxamine threshold
description: Iron poisoning phases: GI (0.5-6 h), latent improvement (6-24 h), shock and metabolic acidosis (12-24 h), hepatotoxicity (2-3 d), pyloric stenosis (4-6 wk). Serum iron at 4-6 h post-ingestion. Whole bowel irrigation if radiopaque pills on AXR. Deferoxamine 15 mg/kg/h IV infusion (max 80 mg/kg/24 h) for: serum iron >90 µmol/L (500 µg/dL), severe symptoms (shock, altered mental status), persistent acidosis, or significant ingestion (>60 mg/kg elemental iron). Urine becomes vin-rose colour with ferrioxamine. Monitor for ARDS at prolonged infusion >24 h.

outcomes.summary: Iron poisoning — deferoxamine if iron >90 µmol/L or severe features
outcomes.detail: Whole bowel irrigation for radiopaque tablets; watch for ARDS at prolonged infusion.

references.label: TOXBASE Iron poisoning monograph

codings.display: Poisoning by iron and its compounds

title: Serotonin syndrome — Hunter criteria and cyproheptadine
description: Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria: in a patient on a serotonergic agent, ONE of: spontaneous clonus, inducible or ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, tremor and hyperreflexia, hypertonia plus T >38°C with clonus. Common precipitants: SSRI/SNRI/MAOI combination, tramadol, linezolid, fentanyl, ondansetron, MDMA, St John's Wort. Treatment: stop all serotonergic drugs; supportive care (IV fluids, cooling, benzodiazepines for agitation); cyproheptadine 12 mg PO then 2 mg every 2 h to 32 mg/day for severe; intubation and paralysis (avoid suxamethonium — hyperkalaemia in rhabdomyolysis) for severe hyperthermia. Avoid antipsychotics (NMS confusion).

outcomes.summary: Serotonin syndrome — stop agents, benzodiazepines, cyproheptadine if severe
outcomes.detail: Differentiate from NMS (hypertonia without clonus, slower onset).

references.label: Dunkley EJC et al. Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria. QJM 2003

codings.display: Adverse effect of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors

title: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome — recognition and management
description: NMS tetrad: hyperthermia, severe muscle rigidity ("lead pipe"), altered mental status, autonomic dysfunction. Develops over 24-72 h after starting/increasing antipsychotic or dopamine withdrawal. CK markedly raised (>1000), leucocytosis. Stop the offending neuroleptic; aggressive cooling; IV fluids and treat rhabdomyolysis (UO 1-2 mL/kg/h); benzodiazepines for agitation. Specific: dantrolene 1-2.5 mg/kg IV every 6 h (rigidity, hyperthermia) and/or bromocriptine 2.5 mg every 6-8 h, amantadine 100 mg BD-TDS. ICU; ECT for refractory/catatonia. Rechallenge with antipsychotic only after 2 weeks recovery, with lower-potency agent.

outcomes.summary: NMS — stop neuroleptic, cool, fluids; dantrolene/bromocriptine if severe
outcomes.detail: Watch rhabdomyolysis and AKI; rechallenge only after recovery with lower-potency agent.

references.label: NICE BNF NMS guidance
Strawn JR et al. NMS. Am J Psychiatry 2007

title: Suspected Wernicke encephalopathy — parenteral thiamine
description: Suspect Wernicke encephalopathy in chronic alcohol use, hyperemesis, malnutrition, post-bariatric surgery, dialysis. Caine criteria — any 2 of: dietary deficiency, oculomotor abnormality, cerebellar dysfunction, altered mental status or memory impairment. Give parenteral thiamine BEFORE any IV glucose (glucose can precipitate Wernicke in deficient patients). Pabrinex IV high-potency 2 pairs three times daily for 3 days, then 1 pair daily for 5 days; orally as B-complex and thiamine thereafter. Treat magnesium deficiency (cofactor).

outcomes.summary: Suspected Wernicke — parenteral thiamine before any glucose
outcomes.detail: Pabrinex high-potency IV 2 pairs TDS × 3 d; correct magnesium.

references.label: Royal College of Physicians Wernicke's encephalopathy guidelines 2013

title: Rhabdomyolysis — aggressive crystalloid and CK monitoring
description: Diagnose with CK ≥5× ULN plus history (trauma, prolonged immobility, exertion, statin, illicit drugs, seizure, NMS/serotonin syndrome). Aggressive IV crystalloid (isotonic) at 1-2 L/h initially aiming UO 200-300 mL/h (1-3 mL/kg/h) until CK trends down.
