Urinary alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate to pH 6.5 is controversial — not routine. Monitor potassium (hyperkalaemia), calcium (hypocalcaemia early, hypercalcaemia late), phosphate, creatinine. Compartment syndrome screen; RRT for AKI/hyperkalaemia/oligo-anuria.

outcomes.summary: Rhabdomyolysis — aggressive isotonic crystalloid to UO 200-300 mL/h
outcomes.detail: Bicarbonate alkalinisation not routine; monitor electrolytes; compartment syndrome screen.

references.label: Bosch X et al. Rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury. NEJM 2009

title: Accidental hypothermia — staged rewarming
description: Swiss staging: HT I (mild 32-35°C, alert, shivering), HT II (moderate 28-32°C, drowsy, no shivering), HT III (severe 24-28°C, unconscious, vital signs present), HT IV (apparent death <24°C). Handle gently — VF on movement. HT I — active external rewarming (warm room, blankets, warm drinks). HT II-III — minimally invasive (warm IV fluids, forced-air warming). HT IV or instability — ECLS/ECMO preferred where available; otherwise continuous CPR and warm lavage. "Not dead until warm and dead" — continue resuscitation to core 32-35°C before declaring death. Avoid drugs and defibrillation until >30°C (but trial defib once at <30°C per ALS).

outcomes.summary: Severe hypothermia — ECMO if cardiac instability; gentle handling
outcomes.detail: "Not dead until warm and dead"; continue CPR to 32-35°C before declaration.

references.label: Resuscitation Council UK ALS — special circumstances: hypothermia 2021

title: Adult acute severe asthma — back-to-back nebs + IV magnesium
description: Severe (any of: PEF 33-50% best/predicted, RR ≥25, HR ≥110, unable to complete sentences) — controlled oxygen for SpO2 94-98%, salbutamol 5 mg + ipratropium 0.5 mg nebulised every 15-20 min, oral prednisolone 40-50 mg or IV hydrocortisone 100 mg. Life-threatening (PEF <33%, SpO2 <92%, silent chest, cyanosis, bradycardia, exhaustion, altered consciousness) — single dose IV magnesium 1.2-2 g over 20 min, consider IV aminophylline 5 mg/kg over 20 min then 0.5 mg/kg/h, or IV salbutamol; involve ICU. Near-fatal (raised PaCO2, requires ventilation) — intubate; ICU.

outcomes.summary: Severe/life-threatening asthma — oxygen, nebs, steroid + IV magnesium
outcomes.detail: Avoid sedation; ICU for life-threatening features.

references.label: BTS/SIGN/NICE Asthma joint guideline 2024

title: COPD exacerbation — NIV criteria for hypercapnic failure
description: Indication for NIV (BiPAP) in COPD exacerbation: persistent hypercapnic respiratory failure (PaCO2 >6 kPa/45 mmHg with pH 7.25-7.35) after 1 hour of optimal medical therapy (controlled O2 target SpO2 88-92%, bronchodilators, prednisolone 30 mg, antibiotics if indicated). Start NIV at 10/4 cmH2O, titrate IPAP up to 20-25 cmH2O over 30-60 min. Repeat ABG at 1 h and 4 h. Failure → intubate if not for ceiling. pH <7.25 — high risk failure, plan early intubation if appropriate. Treat cause: bronchodilators, steroids, antibiotics (Anthonisen criteria), VTE prophylaxis.

outcomes.summary: COPD exacerbation + pH 7.25-7.35 — NIV
outcomes.detail: Persistent pH <7.25 on NIV — intubate if appropriate; controlled O2 target 88-92%.

references.label: BTS/ICS Ventilatory Management of Acute Hypercapnic Respiratory Failure 2016
GOLD 2024

title: Acute bowel obstruction — drip and suck plus surgical triggers
description: Diagnose by abdominal pain, distension, vomiting (early in proximal, late in distal), absolute constipation, and abdominal X-ray/CT showing dilated loops with fluid levels. Drip and suck: NG decompression, IV crystalloid + electrolyte correction (often hypokalaemic alkalosis), strict input/output, NBM, regular review. CT for diagnosis, level, cause, and complications (strangulation, perforation, ischaemia). Operate for: peritonism, signs of strangulation (constant pain, fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, lactate), pneumoperitoneum, closed-loop obstruction, no improvement at 48-72 h of conservative management, virgin abdomen (no prior surgery — adhesions less likely cause).

outcomes.summary: SBO — drip-and-suck; surgery for peritonism, strangulation, virgin abdomen
outcomes.detail: Closed-loop obstruction is an emergency; gastrografin challenge may both diagnose and treat partial.

references.label: WSES guidelines on bowel obstruction 2019

title: Upper GI bleed — Glasgow-Blatchford + Rockall pathway
description: In suspected upper GI bleed calculate Glasgow-Blatchford Score. GBS = 0 — outpatient management is safe. ≥1 — admit; transfuse RBC for Hb <70 g/L (or <80 if cardiac disease); restrictive transfusion strategy (TRICC, Villanueva NEJM 2013). IV PPI infusion for high-risk endoscopic stigmata. Variceal bleed — terlipressin + antibiotics (ceftriaxone 1 g/day for 7 days). Endoscopy within 24 h; <12 h for unstable/variceal. Post-endoscopic Rockall predicts rebleed and mortality.

outcomes.summary: UGIB — Glasgow-Blatchford for triage; OGD within 24 h
outcomes.detail: Restrictive transfusion Hb <70; PPI for high-risk stigmata; variceal — terlipressin + ceftriaxone.

references.label: NICE CG141 Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding in over 16s 2012 (updated)

title: Adult DKA — JBDS-IP fixed-rate insulin protocol
description: Diagnose DKA: blood ketones ≥3 mmol/L (or urine ketones ≥2+), pH <7.3 or HCO3 <15 mmol/L, glucose >11 mmol/L. Fluids: 1 L 0.9% saline over 60 min, then 2nd L over 2 h, 3rd L over 4 h, etc., reassess. Fixed-rate insulin 0.1 U/kg/h IV starting after first litre. Add 10% dextrose at 125 mL/h once glucose <14 mmol/L; continue fixed-rate insulin until ketones <0.6 and HCO3 >18 and pH >7.3. Continue patient's long-acting insulin throughout. K+ replacement per band (3.5-5.5 add 40 mmol/L; <3.5 senior review). Avoid bicarbonate.

outcomes.summary: DKA — fluids + fixed-rate insulin 0.1 U/kg/h + K+ replacement
outcomes.detail: Continue long-acting insulin; switch to dextrose when glucose <14; resolution = ketones <0.6.

references.label: JBDS-IP Management of DKA in Adults 2023

title: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state — JBDS protocol
description: HHS criteria: hypovolaemia, marked hyperglycaemia (>30 mmol/L) without significant ketonaemia (<3) or acidosis (pH >7.3, HCO3 >15), measured osmolality >320 mOsm/kg. Slower fluid resuscitation than DKA: 0.9% saline 1 L in first hour, then 0.5-1 L/h titrated to fall in osmolality 3-8 mOsm/kg/h. INSULIN delayed — start only if glucose not falling with fluids alone, or if significant ketonaemia present (then 0.05 U/kg/h). VTE prophylaxis with LMWH (high VTE risk). Identify and treat precipitant (infection, MI, stroke, drugs).

outcomes.summary: HHS — slower fluids than DKA, delay insulin, LMWH
outcomes.detail: Aim osmolality fall 3-8 mOsm/kg/h; LMWH for VTE; treat precipitant.

references.label: JBDS-IP Management of the Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State (HHS) in Adults 2022 update

codings.display: Type 2 DM with hyperosmolarity without coma

title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage — WFNS grading and aneurysm securing
description: WFNS SAH grading I-V by GCS and motor deficit. Confirm with CT (sensitivity 100% if <6 h); negative CT in delayed presentation — LP at ≥12 h for xanthochromia (visual or spectrophotometric). CT angiography for aneurysm. Treat early (within 24-48 h) — endovascular coiling preferred over surgical clipping per ISAT for amenable aneurysms. Nimodipine 60 mg every 4 h orally for 21 days (reduces ischaemic complications). BP control SBP <160 mmHg until aneurysm secured; aim higher MAP if vasospasm develops (triple-H largely abandoned). Monitor for hydrocephalus (EVD), rebleed, vasospasm (TCD or angiography).

outcomes.summary: SAH — secure aneurysm <24-48 h; nimodipine 21 d
outcomes.detail: Coil over clip per ISAT for amenable; monitor for hydrocephalus, rebleed, vasospasm.

references.label: AHA/ASA Guidelines for the Management of Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage 2023

codings.display: Subarachnoid haemorrhage from intracranial artery, unspecified

title: Adult bacterial meningitis — empirical antibiotics within 1 h
description: Empirical antibiotics for community-acquired bacterial meningitis (after blood cultures, before LP if delay): IV ceftriaxone 2 g (with vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg if penicillin-resistant pneumococcus suspected). Add amoxicillin 2 g every 4 h for Listeria cover in >50 y, alcohol misuse, immunocompromise, pregnancy. Dexamethasone 10 mg every 6 h for 4 days started BEFORE or with first dose of antibiotic — pneumococcal meningitis (de Gans NEJM 2002). Aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 h if encephalitis features. Notify public health; chemoprophylaxis to close contacts (ciprofloxacin/rifampicin).

outcomes.summary: Adult bacterial meningitis — ceftriaxone within 1 h + dexamethasone
outcomes.detail: Add amoxicillin for Listeria cover in elderly/immunocompromised/pregnant.

references.label: NICE NG240 Meningitis (bacterial) and meningococcal disease 2024
IDSA Practice Guidelines for the Management of Bacterial Meningitis 2004

title: Metastatic spinal cord compression — MRI within 24 h and steroid
description: Suspect MSCC in cancer patient or new presentation with severe back pain (worse on lying flat, coughing, straining), radicular pain, weakness, bladder/bowel dysfunction. Whole-spine MRI within 24 hours (sooner if neurology). Start dexamethasone 16 mg loading then 8 mg BD with PPI cover, pending oncology and neurosurgical/radiotherapy decision. Definitive treatment options — decompressive surgery within 24 h for prognosis >3 months and a single level (Patchell trial), radiotherapy for radiosensitive or unsuitable for surgery; analgesia, VTE prophylaxis, bladder management.

outcomes.summary: MSCC — MRI <24 h + dexamethasone 16 mg + neurosurg/oncology
outcomes.detail: Surgery within 24 h if prognosis >3 months; radiotherapy adjunct or alternative.

references.label: NICE NG234 Metastatic spinal cord compression in adults 2023

title: HFrEF — quadruple therapy (4 pillars) initiation
description: For HFrEF (LVEF ≤40%) initiate the four pillars: (1) ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) — superior to ACEi (PARADIGM-HF); (2) beta-blocker (bisoprolol, carvedilol, nebivolol, metoprolol succinate); (3) MRA (spironolactone or eplerenone); (4) SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin DAPA-HF, empagliflozin EMPEROR-Reduced) regardless of diabetes status. Start all four within weeks; titrate every 2 weeks to target or maximum tolerated dose. Monitor U&E and BP. Add loop diuretic for congestion. Discuss devices (CRT for QRS ≥150 ms LBBB; ICD per criteria).

outcomes.summary: HFrEF — start all 4 pillars within weeks of diagnosis
outcomes.detail: ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i; SGLT2i regardless of diabetes; titrate every 2 weeks.

references.label: ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of acute and chronic heart failure 2021 (2023 focused update)
McMurray JJV et al. PARADIGM-HF. NEJM 2014

title: HFpEF — SGLT2 inhibitor as evidence-based therapy
description: For heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (LVEF ≥50%) SGLT2 inhibitors are recommended: empagliflozin (EMPEROR-Preserved) and dapagliflozin (DELIVER). Combine with: loop diuretic for congestion, manage comorbidities (AF, hypertension, obesity, OSA), MRA (spironolactone) considered (TOPCAT post-hoc benefit in lower EF range), control HR <80 in AF. Avoid digoxin unless rate control failure. Cardiac rehab where available.

outcomes.summary: HFpEF — start SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin/empagliflozin)
outcomes.detail: Combine with diuretic for congestion; treat comorbidities; MRA in selected patients.

references.label: Anker SD et al. EMPEROR-Preserved. NEJM 2021
Solomon SD et al. DELIVER. NEJM 2022

title: Type 2 diabetes — SGLT2 vs GLP-1 RA by comorbidity
description: In T2DM use comorbidity-driven second-line selection after metformin. Established ASCVD or high CV risk — GLP-1 RA with proven benefit (semaglutide, liraglutide, dulaglutide) or SGLT2 with proven benefit (empagliflozin, canagliflozin). HFrEF — SGLT2 (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin). CKD with albuminuria — SGLT2 (dapagliflozin DAPA-CKD, empagliflozin EMPA-KIDNEY). Obesity — GLP-1 RA (semaglutide, tirzepatide). Cost constraint — SU or thiazolidinedione where appropriate. Stop SU/insulin titration if hypos. HbA1c target individualised (typically <53 mmol/mol; <58 in elderly/comorbid).

outcomes.summary: T2DM 2nd line — choose by comorbidity (ASCVD, HF, CKD, obesity)
outcomes.detail: GLP-1 RA for ASCVD/obesity; SGLT2 for HF/CKD.

references.label: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes 2024
NICE NG28 Type 2 diabetes in adults 2015 (updated 2022)

title: Type 2 diabetes — treatment intensification ladder (NICE NG28)
description: Step 1: lifestyle + metformin (standard-release titrate to 2 g/day; MR if GI intolerance). Step 2 at HbA1c ≥58 (or ≥48 if no intolerance to combination): add SGLT2 (if CV/renal indication or high CV risk) OR DPP4i / pioglitazone / SU (sitagliptin/alogliptin/linagliptin per NICE TA approval). Step 3: triple therapy or switch to GLP-1 RA (BMI ≥35 with psychosocial impact or BMI <35 if insulin would have significant occupational implications or weight loss benefit specialist input). Step 4: insulin (basal, then prandial). Continue metformin throughout unless contraindicated.

outcomes.summary: T2DM ladder — metformin → SGLT2/DPP4i → triple → insulin
outcomes.detail: Continue metformin unless contraindicated; consider GLP-1 RA per NICE BMI thresholds.

references.label: NICE NG28 Type 2 diabetes 2015 (updated 2022)

title: Hypertension — NICE A/C/D stepwise therapy
description: Step 1 — <55 y or T2DM: ACEi (or ARB if intolerant) ("A"). ≥55 y or African/Caribbean: CCB ("C"). Step 2 — A + C. Step 3 — A + C + thiazide-like diuretic (indapamide preferred) ("D"). Step 4 (resistant): K+ <4.5 — add spironolactone 25 mg; K+ >4.5 — add alpha- or beta-blocker. Confirm diagnosis with ambulatory or home BP. Targets <140/90 (<150/90 in ≥80 y) — recent evidence supports lower targets for cardiovascular benefit; individualise. Investigate secondary causes if young, severe, refractory, or features.

outcomes.summary: Hypertension — A/C/D pathway by age and ethnicity
outcomes.detail: Confirm with ABPM/HBPM; targets individualised; investigate secondary if young/refractory.

references.label: NICE NG136 Hypertension in adults 2019 (updated)

title: Resistant hypertension — spironolactone (PATHWAY-2)
description: Resistant hypertension = BP above target despite three drugs at optimal doses including a diuretic. Confirm adherence and exclude white-coat, secondary causes (primary aldosteronism, renal artery stenosis, OSA, phaeochromocytoma, Cushing's). Add spironolactone 25 mg daily (titrate to 50 mg) — superior to bisoprolol and doxazosin in PATHWAY-2 (Williams Lancet 2015). Monitor K+ and creatinine at 1, 4 weeks. Alternative: amiloride 10-20 mg. Renal denervation an option for select refractory cases. Aldosterone-renin ratio before starting MRA if primary aldosteronism not yet excluded (stop spironolactone 4-6 weeks for accurate testing).

outcomes.summary: Resistant HTN — add spironolactone if K+ <4.5
outcomes.detail: Confirm adherence; exclude secondary causes; monitor K+ on MRA.

references.label: Williams B et al. PATHWAY-2. Lancet 2015

title: CKD risk stratification — eGFR + ACR grid (KDIGO)
description: Stratify CKD using both eGFR (G1 >90, G2 60-89, G3a 45-59, G3b 30-44, G4 15-29, G5 <15) and albumin:creatinine ratio (A1 <3 mg/mmol, A2 3-30, A3 >30). Risk increases across both axes — green/yellow/orange/red zones guide referral and monitoring frequency. Refer nephrology when: eGFR <30, urinary ACR ≥70 mg/mmol, urinary ACR ≥30 with haematuria, sustained decrease eGFR ≥15% in 12 months. Manage: BP <130/80 with ACEi/ARB (with ACR ≥3 in diabetes, ACR ≥30 in non-diabetes), SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin/empagliflozin) with proteinuric CKD even without diabetes, statin, treat anaemia, mineral and bone disorder.

outcomes.summary: CKD — KDIGO grid drives referral and SGLT2 indication
outcomes.detail: SGLT2i for proteinuric CKD without diabetes; nephrology referral by eGFR/ACR thresholds.

references.label: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of CKD
NICE NG203 Chronic kidney disease 2021

title: CKD-mineral bone disorder — phosphate, calcium, PTH targets
description: In CKD-MBD aim phosphate within normal range; calcium within normal range; PTH 2-9× upper limit of normal in dialysis (no firm target pre-dialysis but trend matters). Step 1 — dietary phosphate restriction. Step 2 — phosphate binders: calcium-based (cautious if high Ca or vascular calcification), non-calcium based (sevelamer, lanthanum). Vitamin D analogues (alfacalcidol, calcitriol) or selective VDR activators (paricalcitol) for hyperparathyroidism. Cinacalcet for refractory SHPT. Parathyroidectomy for severe refractory or symptomatic SHPT. Avoid bisphosphonates in eGFR <30.

outcomes.summary: CKD-MBD — phosphate/Ca/PTH targets and stepwise therapy
outcomes.detail: Avoid bisphosphonates in eGFR <30; cinacalcet for refractory SHPT.

references.label: KDIGO 2017 Update on CKD-MBD

title: COPD — GOLD 2024 ABE assessment and treatment
description: GOLD 2024 simplified groups: Group A — low symptoms (mMRC 0-1 or CAT <10), low exacerbation risk → bronchodilator (LAMA or LABA). Group B — high symptoms, low exacerbation risk → LAMA + LABA. Group E — high exacerbation risk (≥2 moderate or ≥1 hospitalisation in last year) → LAMA + LABA, add ICS if blood eosinophils ≥300 cells/μL. Triple therapy (LAMA + LABA + ICS) for persistent exacerbations on dual bronchodilator. Roflumilast for chronic bronchitis + FEV1 <50%; azithromycin 250 mg three times weekly for selected non-smokers with persistent exacerbations.

outcomes.summary: COPD — GOLD ABE; ICS only if eosinophils ≥300 or persistent exacerbations
outcomes.detail: Avoid routine ICS in COPD without exacerbation/eosinophil indication (pneumonia risk).

references.label: GOLD 2024 Global Strategy for Diagnosis, Management, and Prevention of COPD

title: Asthma — GINA 2024 ICS-formoterol as reliever
description: GINA 2024 recommends ICS-formoterol as preferred reliever in all asthma severities to reduce exacerbation risk; SABA-only treatment is no longer recommended. Track 1 (preferred): Steps 1-2 use as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol. Step 3-4 maintenance + reliever therapy (MART) with low-/medium-dose ICS-formoterol. Step 5 add LAMA (e.g. tiotropium), consider biologics for severe eosinophilic/Type 2 asthma. Track 2 (alternative) — daily ICS + as-needed SABA, escalating ICS dose and adding LABA/LAMA. Confirm spirometry, review inhaler technique, adherence, comorbidities and triggers at each step.

outcomes.summary: Asthma — ICS-formoterol reliever preferred; avoid SABA-only
outcomes.detail: MART for steps 3-4; biologics for severe Type 2 asthma at step 5.

references.label: GINA Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention 2024

title: Severe asthma — biologic selection by phenotype
description: Refer to severe asthma service for biologic eligibility. Allergic phenotype (IgE 30-1500, perennial allergen sensitisation) — omalizumab. Eosinophilic (blood eos ≥300 cells/μL plus exacerbations) — mepolizumab (anti-IL5) or benralizumab (anti-IL5Rα) or reslizumab. Eosinophilic ± Type 2 (high FeNO, atopic) — dupilumab (anti-IL4Rα; not in helminth-endemic without deworming). Tezepelumab (anti-TSLP) — broad efficacy across phenotypes including low-Th2. Confirm adherence, technique, comorbidities. Continue ICS at lower step where possible.

outcomes.summary: Severe asthma — phenotype-matched biologic
outcomes.detail: Omalizumab for allergic; anti-IL5 family for eosinophilic; dupilumab for Type 2; tezepelumab broad.

references.label: BTS Difficult Asthma Network position statement 2024
GINA 2024 — Severe asthma

codings.display: Severe persistent asthma with status asthmaticus

title: Obstructive sleep apnoea — STOP-BANG screening
description: STOP-BANG: Snoring loudly, Tiredness, Observed apnoea, high blood Pressure, BMI >35, Age >50, Neck >40 cm, male Gender. 0-2 low risk; 3-4 intermediate; ≥5 high risk for moderate-severe OSA. Refer for sleep study (home polygraphy or in-lab polysomnography) if ≥3 plus daytime sleepiness, or ≥5 regardless. Treat by AHI: mild (5-14) lifestyle/positional/MAD; moderate-severe (≥15) CPAP first-line. Address obesity (consider weight-loss intervention). Pre-operative screening for high-risk surgery candidates.

outcomes.summary: STOP-BANG ≥3 with symptoms — refer for sleep study
outcomes.detail: CPAP first-line moderate-severe; MAD/lifestyle for mild; address obesity.

references.label: NICE NG202 Obstructive sleep apnoea/hypopnoea syndrome 2021

title: Obesity pharmacotherapy — eligibility and agents
description: Consider obesity pharmacotherapy when lifestyle intervention is insufficient and BMI ≥30 (or ≥27 with comorbidity). Semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly SC (Wegovy STEP trials — ~15% weight loss). Tirzepatide weekly SC (GIP/GLP-1; SURMOUNT — up to 20% weight loss). Liraglutide 3 mg daily SC. Orlistat 120 mg three times daily with meals (modest effect, GI side-effects). Naltrexone-bupropion (avoid in seizure disorder, uncontrolled HTN). Phentermine-topiramate (not licensed in UK). Continue indefinitely with monitoring; weight rebounds on discontinuation. Bariatric referral for BMI ≥40 (or ≥35 with comorbidity).

outcomes.summary: Obesity — pharmacotherapy as adjunct to lifestyle, lifelong
outcomes.detail: Semaglutide/tirzepatide most efficacious; weight rebounds on discontinuation; bariatric referral for BMI ≥40.

references.label: NICE TA875 Semaglutide for managing overweight and obesity 2023
NICE TA1026 Tirzepatide for managing overweight and obesity 2024

title: Secondary prevention — high-intensity statin post-MI
description: Offer high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80 mg or rosuvastatin 20-40 mg) for secondary prevention after MI, ACS, ischaemic stroke/TIA, PAD, or established cardiovascular disease. Target LDL-C reduction ≥40% from baseline, or LDL-C <1.8 mmol/L (<1.4 in very high risk per ESC). Add ezetimibe 10 mg if target not reached (IMPROVE-IT). PCSK9 inhibitor (alirocumab/evolocumab) or inclisiran for very high risk not at target on maximum tolerated statin + ezetimibe. Statin intolerance: rotate (1-2 trials), low-dose intermittent, bempedoic acid.

outcomes.summary: Post-MI/ACS/stroke — high-intensity statin
outcomes.detail: Target LDL <1.8 (<1.4 very high risk); ezetimibe + PCSK9i if not at target.

references.label: ESC Guidelines on cardiovascular disease prevention 2021
NICE CG181 Cardiovascular disease: risk assessment and reduction 2014 (updated)

title: Familial hypercholesterolaemia — screening and PCSK9i pathway
description: Suspect heterozygous FH if untreated LDL-C >4.9 mmol/L in adult or >4.0 mmol/L in child, especially with family history of premature CHD or tendon xanthomas. Use Dutch Lipid Clinic Network criteria or Simon Broome. Refer for cascade testing of first-degree relatives. Treat with high-intensity statin from age 8-10 in confirmed FH; add ezetimibe and PCSK9 inhibitor (alirocumab/evolocumab) or inclisiran if LDL-C not <2.6 mmol/L (primary prevention) or <1.8 (secondary prevention/very high risk). Homozygous FH — refer specialist centre; LDL apheresis, evinacumab.

outcomes.summary: Suspected FH — refer + cascade test family
outcomes.detail: High-intensity statin from age 8-10; PCSK9i/inclisiran if not at target.

references.label: NICE CG71 Familial hypercholesterolaemia 2008 (updated 2019)

title: CVD primary prevention — QRISK3 ≥10% offer statin
description: Calculate QRISK3 in adults 25-84 years (not in known CVD, T1DM, eGFR <60, hereditary lipid disorder). Offer atorvastatin 20 mg primary prevention if 10-year CVD risk ≥10%, after lifestyle discussion. Consider if 5-9% with shared decision making, particularly with risk modifiers (FH, ethnic minority, severe mental illness, CKD, autoimmune disease, SLE, RA). Discuss benefits and risks (NNT, side effects). Repeat QRISK3 every 5 years (more often if changes); BP and lipid monitoring. Atherosclerotic imaging (CT coronary artery calcium) selectively.

outcomes.summary: QRISK3 ≥10% — offer statin after shared decision
outcomes.detail: 5-9% — consider with risk modifiers; reassess every 5 years.

references.label: NICE CG181 Cardiovascular disease: risk assessment and reduction 2014 (updated)

codings.display: Encounter for screening for cardiovascular disorders

title: Smoking cessation — varenicline, NRT, bupropion
description: Offer behavioural support plus pharmacotherapy. First-line varenicline 0.5 mg OD escalating to 1 mg BD for 12 weeks; or combination NRT (long-acting patch + short-acting gum/lozenge/inhalator); or bupropion 150 mg OD escalating to 150 mg BD. Varenicline highest quit rate in head-to-head trials (e.g. EAGLES). Consider cytisinicline as an alternative where available. E-cigarettes can be used as an aid to cessation when other agents have failed (NICE NG209). Continue NRT during pregnancy if behavioural support insufficient. Annual cessation prompts at every smoker visit.

outcomes.summary: Smoking cessation — varenicline + behavioural support first-line
outcomes.detail: Combination NRT alternative; bupropion if SSRI contraindicated; e-cigarettes per NG209.

references.label: NICE NG209 Tobacco: preventing uptake, promoting quitting and treating dependence 2021
Anthenelli RM et al. EAGLES. Lancet 2016

title: Alcohol — AUDIT screening, brief intervention, and pharmacotherapy
description: Use AUDIT-C (3 items) for screening — score ≥5 (men) or ≥4 (women) suggests harmful drinking; full AUDIT for stratification (8-15 hazardous, 16-19 harmful, ≥20 likely dependence). Brief intervention (5-15 min FRAMES) for hazardous and harmful drinking. Pharmacotherapy for dependence: naltrexone (avoid in opioid use), acamprosate (start within 1 week of abstinence), nalmefene (reduction goal). Disulfiram in supervised settings. Detox planning — outpatient if mild-moderate, inpatient if severe (high CIWA-Ar) or comorbidity; chlordiazepoxide/diazepam reducing regimen; thiamine.

outcomes.summary: AUDIT-positive — brief intervention; dependence — pharmacotherapy
outcomes.detail: Naltrexone/acamprosate first-line; inpatient detox if severe/comorbid.

references.label: NICE CG115 Alcohol-use disorders: diagnosis, assessment and management 2011

title: Opioid use disorder — buprenorphine, methadone, naltrexone
description: Offer opioid substitution treatment (OST) — first-line buprenorphine (or buprenorphine-naloxone) titrated from 8-16 mg/day to 16-24 mg/day; or methadone titrated from 10-30 mg to 60-120 mg/day. Both reduce mortality (e.g. NSDU Cochrane). Use long-acting depot buprenorphine where available for retention. Oral or extended-release naltrexone for selected abstinent patients motivated to remain opioid-free. Provide harm reduction (clean needles, safer use, take-home naloxone), HIV/HCV testing and treatment, comorbid mental health support. Treat in long-term, integrated programme rather than detox alone.

outcomes.summary: OUD — offer buprenorphine or methadone (OST) long-term
outcomes.detail: Naloxone take-home, HIV/HCV testing, integrated care; depot buprenorphine where available.

references.label: NICE CG52 Drug misuse in over 16s: opioid detoxification 2007 (updated)
WHO Guidelines for the psychosocially assisted pharmacological treatment of opioid dependence 2009

title: Osteoporosis — FRAX and treatment thresholds
description: Calculate FRAX 10-year fracture risk in postmenopausal women and men ≥50. Treat osteoporosis (T-score ≤-2.5 on DEXA OR fragility fracture) with calcium/vitamin D plus oral bisphosphonate (alendronate 70 mg weekly, risedronate 35 mg weekly) first-line. Zoledronate 5 mg IV yearly if oral intolerance/non-adherence. Denosumab 60 mg SC every 6 months (do NOT stop without follow-on therapy — rebound vertebral fractures). Anabolic agents (teriparatide, romosozumab) for severe/very high-risk fracture history. Reassess bisphosphonate holiday at 5 years oral or 3 years IV.

outcomes.summary: Osteoporosis — bisphosphonate + Ca/vit D; denosumab needs follow-on
outcomes.detail: Stopping denosumab without sequential therapy risks rebound vertebral fractures.

references.label: NICE TA464 Bisphosphonates for treating osteoporosis 2017
ROS UK Clinical Guidance 2022

codings.display: Age-related osteoporosis without current pathological fracture

title: Diabetes monitoring — HbA1c targets and intervals
description: Check HbA1c every 3 months when not at target or recent change; every 6 months when stable at target. Target HbA1c <53 mmol/mol (7%) for most adults; <48 mmol/mol (6.5%) in newly diagnosed with low hypoglycaemia risk; <58-64 mmol/mol (7.5-8%) in elderly with limited life expectancy, hypoglycaemia, comorbidity. Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) for T1DM and insulin-treated T2DM with hypoglycaemia/awareness loss. Diabetes Annual Review: HbA1c, BP, lipids, BMI, U&E + ACR, foot exam, retinal screening, smoking, mood (PHQ-2/9), erectile dysfunction.

outcomes.summary: Diabetes — HbA1c every 3-6 months; annual review bundle
outcomes.detail: Individualise target by age and comorbidity; CGM for selected patients.

references.label: NICE NG28 Type 2 diabetes 2015 (updated 2022)
NICE NG17 Type 1 diabetes 2015 (updated)

title: Diabetes foot — annual risk stratification and referral
description: Annual diabetes foot exam: 10g monofilament, vibration, foot pulses, deformity, skin, footwear, callus. Stratify risk: low (no risk factors); moderate (deformity, neuropathy, or non-critical ischaemia); high (previous ulcer/amputation, ESRF, multiple risk factors, neuropathy + deformity or PVD); active foot disease (ulceration, infection, Charcot, gangrene). Refer to specialist multidisciplinary foot team within 24 h for active foot disease; 2-4 weeks for high-risk review. Education on daily foot inspection, appropriate footwear, foot hygiene.

outcomes.summary: Active diabetic foot — MDT referral within 24 hours
outcomes.detail: Annual screening; education on daily inspection and footwear.

references.label: NICE NG19 Diabetic foot problems 2015 (updated 2019)

title: Rheumatoid arthritis — treat to target with early DMARD
description: In early RA start DMARD (methotrexate 15-25 mg/week oral or SC) within 3 months of persistent synovitis, with bridging glucocorticoid (oral or IM) for symptom control. Add second conventional DMARD if not at target (DAS28 <2.6 remission, or low disease activity) by 6 months. Step up to biologic DMARD (TNF inhibitor first-line) or JAK inhibitor at 6 months if persistent active disease. Folate 5 mg weekly with methotrexate. Baseline pre-biologic: hepatitis B/C, TB screen, pregnancy, vaccines. Continue treat-to-target reviews every 1-3 months until target reached.

outcomes.summary: Early RA — DMARD within 3 months, treat-to-target
outcomes.detail: Methotrexate first-line; biologic at 6 months if still active; baseline TB/HBV/HCV screen.

references.label: EULAR recommendations for the management of rheumatoid arthritis 2022 update
NICE NG100 Rheumatoid arthritis in adults 2018

title: Gout — urate-lowering therapy with treat-to-target
description: Offer urate-lowering therapy (ULT) after first or recurrent attack to all patients with: ≥2 flares per year, tophi, urate arthropathy, urate renal stones, CKD, diuretic use, or young age at onset. Allopurinol first-line — start at 100 mg/day (50 mg if eGFR <60), titrate by 100 mg monthly to serum urate <360 µmol/L (<300 µmol/L if tophi). Add colchicine 500 mcg OD/BD or NSAID prophylaxis during titration to prevent flares for 6 months. Febuxostat second-line (caution in established CV disease — CARES). Test HLA-B*5801 in high-risk ethnicities (Han Chinese, Thai, Korean) before allopurinol — Stevens-Johnson risk.

outcomes.summary: Gout — allopurinol titrate to urate <360 µmol/L
outcomes.detail: Flare prophylaxis during titration; HLA-B*5801 in high-risk groups before allopurinol.

references.label: EULAR evidence-based recommendations for the management of gout 2016
BSR Guideline for the management of gout 2017

title: Osteoarthritis — exercise first, topical NSAID, surgery selectively
description: First-line for hip/knee OA: structured exercise programme and weight loss if overweight. Topical NSAID for knee or hand OA before oral. Oral NSAID at lowest effective dose for shortest period, with PPI if GI risk. Paracetamol — NICE 2022 no longer recommends as first-line (limited efficacy in OA). Intra-articular steroid for severe acute flares of knee. Consider physiotherapy. Joint replacement when symptoms reduce quality of life despite non-operative treatment; BMI is not an absolute barrier. Glucosamine, chondroitin, hyaluronate not recommended.

outcomes.summary: OA — exercise + weight loss; topical NSAID before oral
outcomes.detail: Paracetamol not first-line; joint replacement when QoL impaired despite conservative treatment.

references.label: NICE NG226 Osteoarthritis in over 16s 2022

title: Primary hypothyroidism — levothyroxine titration
description: Levothyroxine 1.6 mcg/kg/day full replacement in young/healthy; start lower (25-50 mcg) and titrate in elderly (>65) or ischaemic heart disease. Recheck TSH 6-8 weeks after dose change; adjust 12.5-25 mcg increments. Aim TSH within reference range (typically 0.4-4.0 mU/L; lower target 0.5-2.5 in pregnancy or trying to conceive). Take on empty stomach 30-60 min before food, 4 h apart from calcium, iron, antacids, statins. Liothyronine combination not routinely; use in select symptomatic patients only with specialist input.

outcomes.summary: Hypothyroidism — levothyroxine titrate by TSH at 6-8 weeks
outcomes.detail: Lower starting dose in elderly/IHD; pregnancy target TSH 0.5-2.5; absorption interactions.

references.label: NICE NG145 Thyroid disease: assessment and management 2019
ATA Guidelines 2014

title: Graves' disease — ATD, radioiodine, or thyroidectomy
description: Graves' disease treatment options: (1) Antithyroid drug (carbimazole 20-40 mg/day initially then titrate; or methimazole; propylthiouracil in first trimester pregnancy or thyroid storm) for 12-18 months — ~40% sustained remission. (2) Radioiodine I-131 — definitive, contraindicated in pregnancy/breastfeeding/active ophthalmopathy. (3) Thyroidectomy — definitive, for large goitre, suspicious nodule, ophthalmopathy, pregnancy unable to use ATD, child preferences. All routes likely lead to lifelong levothyroxine after radioiodine or surgery. Beta-blocker (propranolol) for symptom control. Smoking cessation important (worsens ophthalmopathy).

outcomes.summary: Graves — ATD vs RAI vs surgery; smoking cessation; beta-blocker for symptoms
outcomes.detail: RAI avoided in active ophthalmopathy; PTU only in 1st trimester pregnancy and thyroid storm.

references.label: ATA Guidelines for Diagnosis and Management of Hyperthyroidism 2016

codings.display: Thyrotoxicosis with diffuse goitre without thyrotoxic crisis

title: Subclinical hypothyroidism — treatment thresholds
description: Treat with levothyroxine when: TSH ≥10 mU/L on two readings 3 months apart, OR persistent symptoms (and TSH ≥7 in <70 y after at least 6 months), OR pregnant/trying to conceive (TSH 2.5-4 lower threshold). Reassess at 6-8 weeks. Do NOT treat asymptomatic mild subclinical hypothyroidism in elderly (>65) — increased atrial fibrillation and osteoporosis with no clear cardiovascular benefit (TRUST trial NEJM 2017). Repeat TSH in 6 months for monitoring if not treating.

outcomes.summary: Subclinical hypothyroidism — treat if TSH ≥10 or pregnancy
outcomes.detail: No benefit to treating asymptomatic elderly with TSH <10.

references.label: Stott DJ et al. TRUST. NEJM 2017
NICE NG145 Thyroid disease 2019

title: PCOS — Rotterdam criteria and management
description: Rotterdam criteria: 2 of 3 — oligo/anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound (≥20 follicles per ovary or ovarian volume ≥10 mL using modern transducers). Exclude differential (CAH, Cushing's, thyroid). Manage by goal: contraception/cycle regulation — combined hormonal contraceptive; hirsutism — CHC plus spironolactone or eflornithine; fertility — letrozole first-line (superior to clomifene PCOSI), metformin adjunct, weight loss; metabolic — annual OGTT/HbA1c, lipid screen, BP, weight, OSA screen.

outcomes.summary: PCOS — Rotterdam criteria; manage by goal (contraception, hirsutism, fertility, metabolic)
outcomes.detail: Letrozole first-line for fertility; annual metabolic screen.

references.label: 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of PCOS (Monash)

title: HRT for menopause — shared decision and risk-benefit
description: Offer HRT to women with vasomotor or genitourinary symptoms of menopause. Combined HRT (oestrogen + progestogen) if uterus present; oestrogen-only if hysterectomy. Transdermal oestrogen preferred for higher VTE risk (no excess VTE), migraine with aura, hypertension, GI disease. Risks: small increased breast cancer risk (oestrogen-progestogen with longer use), VTE (oral only), stroke (oral); benefits include reduced osteoporosis, possibly cardiovascular if started <60 y or within 10 years of menopause. Avoid in active breast cancer, VTE history, hormone-sensitive cancer, unexplained PV bleed. Vaginal oestrogen for GSM has minimal systemic absorption — safe long-term.

outcomes.summary: HRT — shared decision; transdermal preferred for higher-risk profiles
outcomes.detail: Vaginal oestrogen safe for GSM long-term; avoid systemic HRT in active hormone-sensitive cancer.

references.label: NICE NG23 Menopause: diagnosis and management 2015 (updated 2019)

title: Knee osteoarthritis — intra-articular corticosteroid for acute flare
description: Intra-articular corticosteroid (e.g. methylprednisolone 40 mg or triamcinolone 40 mg) provides short-term pain relief in moderate-severe knee OA flare unresponsive to oral/topical analgesia. Use sparingly (no more than 3-4 per joint per year — risk of accelerated cartilage loss with frequent injection). No long-term structural benefit. Inform patients of transient flare 24-48 h post-injection. Avoid in suspected joint infection. Hyaluronic acid (viscosupplementation) NOT recommended by NICE.

outcomes.summary: Knee OA flare — single intra-articular steroid; no more than 3-4/year
outcomes.detail: No long-term structural benefit; hyaluronic acid not recommended.

references.label: NICE NG226 Osteoarthritis in over 16s 2022

codings.display: Unilateral primary osteoarthritis of unspecified knee

title: Stable angina — antianginal therapy ladder
description: All patients with stable angina: aspirin 75-100 mg, high-intensity statin, ACEi if hypertension/diabetes/CKD, lifestyle and risk factor modification. First-line symptomatic: beta-blocker (bisoprolol, atenolol) OR calcium channel blocker (verapamil/diltiazem rate-limiting if no LV dysfunction; or amlodipine). Step up combination if monotherapy insufficient. Second-line agents: long-acting nitrate, nicorandil, ivabradine (HR ≥70 sinus), ranolazine. GTN spray for symptom relief. Consider revascularisation (PCI or CABG) for symptoms refractory to optimal medical therapy, or specific anatomic indications (LM, proximal LAD, multi-vessel with diabetes).

outcomes.summary: Stable angina — beta-blocker or CCB first; revascularise if refractory
outcomes.detail: Secondary prevention with aspirin + statin + ACEi/ARB; nitrates and ranolazine second-line.

references.label: ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of chronic coronary syndromes 2024
NICE CG126 Stable angina 2011

title: Peripheral arterial disease — Best Medical Therapy and supervised exercise
description: PAD diagnosis: ABI ≤0.9 with claudication or asymptomatic. Best medical therapy: smoking cessation (most important), statin (atorvastatin 80 mg), antiplatelet (aspirin 75 mg or clopidogrel 75 mg — CAPRIE), ACEi if hypertension. Supervised exercise programme (at least 30 min, 3 times/week, 12 weeks). Cilostazol 100 mg BD if intolerant of exercise. Revascularisation (angioplasty/stent or bypass) for lifestyle-limiting claudication despite BMT or critical limb ischaemia (rest pain, tissue loss). Manage diabetes; foot care.

outcomes.summary: PAD — smoking cessation + statin + antiplatelet + supervised exercise
outcomes.detail: Revascularisation for lifestyle-limiting or critical limb ischaemia.

references.label: ESC Guidelines on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Peripheral Arterial Diseases 2017 (focused update)
NICE CG147 PAD 2012

title: Severe aortic stenosis — SAVR vs TAVI
description: Severe AS = aortic Vmax ≥4 m/s, mean gradient ≥40 mmHg, AVA ≤1 cm². Intervention indicated when symptoms or LVEF <50% or undergoing other cardiac surgery. TAVI now preferred over surgical AVR for: high or intermediate surgical risk; age ≥75 (ESC 2021); patient with anatomy suitable for transfemoral approach. SAVR preferred for low-risk young patients, mechanical valve preference (lifelong anticoagulation), bicuspid valve, concomitant ascending aortic disease, severely calcified annulus. Asymptomatic severe AS with very high gradient, rapid progression, or exercise-induced symptoms — early intervention considered.

outcomes.summary: Symptomatic severe AS — TAVI vs SAVR per heart team
outcomes.detail: TAVI preferred for ≥75 with suitable anatomy; SAVR for younger, bicuspid, ascending aorta disease.

references.label: ESC/EACTS Guidelines for the Management of Valvular Heart Disease 2021

title: Severe primary mitral regurgitation — early intervention
description: In severe primary (degenerative) MR offer surgery (preferably mitral valve repair, not replacement) when symptoms or LV dilatation (LVESD ≥40 mm) or LVEF 30-60%, or new AF or pulmonary hypertension. In asymptomatic patient with low surgical risk and high likelihood of durable repair (e.g. specialist heart valve centre), early surgery to preserve LV function. TEER (transcatheter edge-to-edge repair, MitraClip) for high surgical risk or selected secondary MR (COAPT). Heart team approach for complex anatomy.

outcomes.summary: Severe primary MR — repair preferred when symptomatic or LV remodelling
outcomes.detail: TEER for high surgical risk; specialist heart valve centre for asymptomatic early repair.

references.label: ESC/EACTS Guidelines for the Management of Valvular Heart Disease 2021

title: Adult depression — pharmacotherapy ladder
description: First-line antidepressant for adult major depression: SSRI (sertraline 50-200 mg or citalopram 20-40 mg or escitalopram 10-20 mg) with psychological therapy where appropriate. Review at 2 and 4 weeks. Switch within class or to another SSRI/SNRI at 4-6 weeks if no response. Second-line: SNRI (venlafaxine, duloxetine), mirtazapine. Third-line: combination (e.g. SSRI + mirtazapine), augmentation with lithium or atypical antipsychotic, or refer specialist. Continue at therapeutic dose for at least 6 months after remission (≥2 years if recurrent or risk factors). Taper to reduce discontinuation symptoms.

outcomes.summary: Adult depression — SSRI first; review at 2 and 4 weeks
outcomes.detail: Continue ≥6 months after remission; switch/augment for non-response.

references.label: NICE NG222 Depression in adults: treatment and management 2022

codings.display: Major depressive disorder, single episode, unspecified

title: Glaucoma — risk factors and timely referral
description: Refer urgently to ophthalmology for: acute angle closure glaucoma (red painful eye, fixed dilated pupil, halos), IOP ≥30 mmHg, visual field defects, suspicious optic disc cupping. Routine referral for primary open-angle glaucoma suspect (IOP 21-29, family history, age >40, African/Caribbean ethnicity, diabetes, high myopia). First-line topical: prostaglandin analogue (latanoprost) once daily. Adherence is the leading cause of treatment failure. Selective laser trabeculoplasty considered as first-line in newly diagnosed (LiGHT trial).

outcomes.summary: Glaucoma — refer per IOP, optic disc, field defect, family history
outcomes.detail: PGA topical first-line; SLT as alternative first-line per LiGHT.

references.label: NICE NG81 Glaucoma 2017 (updated 2022)
Gazzard G et al. LiGHT Trial. Lancet 2019

title: IBD flare — prednisolone or biologic stepwise approach
description: Acute severe ulcerative colitis (Truelove and Witts ≥6 bloody stools/day + ≥1 systemic feature) — admit, IV hydrocortisone 100 mg every 6 h, VTE prophylaxis (high risk), assess at day 3 (Oxford criteria: stool ≥8, or 3-8 plus CRP ≥45) — rescue with infliximab 5 mg/kg or ciclosporin. Surgery (colectomy) if no response by day 7. Crohn's flare: assess severity, prednisolone 30-40 mg taper or budesonide for ileocaecal disease, biologics (anti-TNF, vedolizumab, ustekinumab, risankizumab) for steroid-dependent/refractory. Maintenance: avoid long-term steroids; thiopurines, biologics. Always: bone protection, infection screen, opportunistic infection prevention pre-biologic.

outcomes.summary: Acute severe UC — IV steroids, day-3 rescue criteria, colectomy by day 7 if no response
outcomes.detail: Crohn's flare — pred + biologic; VTE prophylaxis; bone protection.

references.label: BSG Guidelines on the management of inflammatory bowel disease in adults 2019 (with updates)

title: Coeliac disease — serological screen and biopsy confirmation
description: Test for coeliac disease (whilst on gluten-containing diet) in: persistent unexplained abdominal/GI symptoms, IBS, faltering growth, prolonged fatigue, unexplained weight loss, severe persistent mouth ulcers, iron/B12/folate deficiency anaemia, T1DM, autoimmune thyroid disease, first-degree relative with coeliac. Test tTG-IgA and total IgA. If positive — refer for endoscopy and duodenal biopsy (≥4 from second part of duodenum + 1 from bulb). Biopsy now omitted by some pathways if tTG-IgA ≥10× ULN, positive EMA, and consistent symptoms (no-biopsy pathway). Strict gluten-free diet for life; calcium, vitamin D, B12, folate, iron status; DEXA at diagnosis.

outcomes.summary: Suspected coeliac — tTG-IgA + total IgA; biopsy or no-biopsy pathway
outcomes.detail: Test on gluten-containing diet; lifelong GFD; bone health and nutritional follow-up.

references.label: NICE NG20 Coeliac disease 2015 (updated 2020)
BSG Guidelines on the diagnosis and management of adult coeliac disease 2014

title: Chronic cough (>8 weeks) — systematic workup
description: Chronic cough >8 weeks — exclude alarm features (haemoptysis, weight loss, breathlessness, persistent fever, abnormal exam/CXR — 2-week pathway). Common causes: upper airway cough syndrome (postnasal drip; trial intranasal steroid/antihistamine), cough-variant asthma (peak flow diary, FeNO, spirometry, trial ICS), GORD (PPI 8-12 weeks, weight loss, lifestyle), ACEi cough (stop ACEi, replace with ARB), idiopathic chronic refractory cough (consider gabapentin/pregabalin or low-dose morphine in specialist clinic). Investigate persistent or red-flag cough with CT thorax.

outcomes.summary: Chronic cough — systematic trial of UACS/asthma/GORD treatment; stop ACEi
outcomes.detail: Investigate red flags with CT; refractory — specialist input.

references.label: BTS Guidelines: Cough in adults 2006 (with updates)
ERS Guidelines on the diagnosis and management of chronic cough 2020

title: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis — antifibrotic therapy
description: Confirm IPF via MDT (clinical + HRCT UIP pattern ± biopsy). Treat with antifibrotic agent: pirfenidone 801 mg TDS (titrate over 14 days) or nintedanib 150 mg BD — both slow FVC decline. Monitor LFT (both), photosensitivity and GI symptoms (pirfenidone), diarrhoea (nintedanib). Vaccinations (pneumococcal, influenza, COVID), pulmonary rehabilitation, oxygen for hypoxia, anti-reflux for symptomatic GORD. Refer to lung transplant centre early (FVC <80% or DLCO <40% on diagnosis). Manage acute exacerbations supportively; high-dose steroids per local protocols.

outcomes.summary: IPF — pirfenidone or nintedanib; early transplant referral
outcomes.detail: Slow FVC decline; vaccinate; refer transplant centre early.

references.label: ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT Clinical Practice Guideline: Treatment of Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis 2015 (updated 2022)

title: Penicillin allergy — delabelling pathway
description: Up to 90% of patients labelled "penicillin-allergic" can tolerate penicillins after structured assessment. Take detailed history: agent, age at reaction, time interval (immediate <1 h vs delayed), nature (rash type, anaphylaxis, organ-specific, severe cutaneous adverse reaction — SJS/TEN/DRESS/AGEP), tolerated alternatives. Low-risk reactions (vague history, distant childhood, mild non-IgE rash, GI upset) — direct oral challenge, consider penicillin VK 250 mg test dose with observation. Moderate-risk — skin testing. SCAR — do not rechallenge. Document outcome in record clearly. Successful delabelling enables narrower antibiotic choices, lower mortality and shorter stays.

outcomes.summary: Penicillin allergy — assess for delabelling
outcomes.detail: Low-risk: oral challenge; moderate-risk: skin testing; SCAR: never rechallenge.

references.label: BSACI guidelines for the management of suspected penicillin allergy 2024

title: Antibiotic de-escalation — culture-directed therapy at 48-72 h
description: Review every patient on empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics at 48-72 hours when culture and sensitivity data return. De-escalate to the narrowest effective agent that covers the identified organism(s). Stop antibiotics with no longer-required cover. Examples: vancomycin → flucloxacillin once MSSA confirmed; piperacillin-tazobactam → amoxicillin once susceptible enterococcus; meropenem → ceftriaxone once Pseudomonas excluded.

outcomes.summary: Antibiotic review at 48-72 h — de-escalate by cultures
outcomes.detail: Stop or narrow per sensitivities; document decision and duration.

references.label: NICE NG15 Antimicrobial stewardship 2015 (updated)

title: Antibiotic duration — short-course evidence base
description: Use the shortest evidence-based duration. CAP — 5 days (or 3 days if afebrile and clinically improving by day 3); HAP — 7 days; uncomplicated UTI women — 3 days nitrofurantoin/trimethoprim/pivmecillinam (or 5 days nitrofurantoin); pyelonephritis — 7 days ciprofloxacin or 10 days co-amoxiclav/cefalexin; cellulitis — 5-7 days; intra-abdominal infection with adequate source control — 4 days (STOP-IT); osteomyelitis — 6 weeks (vs longer historic); bacterial endocarditis — full course per organism. Spellberg-led evidence: shorter is non-inferior with less resistance and fewer side-effects.

outcomes.summary: Antibiotic course — match evidence-based duration
outcomes.detail: CAP 5 d, UTI 3 d, cellulitis 5-7 d, intra-abdominal 4 d post source control.

references.label: Spellberg B. The new antibiotic mantra: shorter is better. JAMA Intern Med 2016
NICE antimicrobial prescribing guidelines (multiple)

title: IV-to-PO switch — criteria at 48 h
description: Review IV antibiotic at 48 hours. Switch to oral when: clinical improvement, afebrile for 24 h, observations stabilising, tolerating oral intake/fluid, no malabsorption, no deep-seated infection requiring high tissue levels (endocarditis, CNS, deep abscess without drainage, S. aureus bacteraemia). Choose oral agent with high bioavailability where possible (e.g. ciprofloxacin, linezolid, fluconazole, metronidazole, doxycycline, levofloxacin). Reduces line complications, cost, length of stay.

outcomes.summary: IV-to-PO switch at 48 h when criteria met
outcomes.detail: Choose agent with high bioavailability; reduces line risk and LOS.

references.label: NICE NG15 Antimicrobial stewardship 2015

title: Clostridioides difficile infection — recognition and testing
description: Test for CDI in hospitalised patients with ≥3 unformed stools in 24 h and antibiotic exposure within last 12 weeks, or new-onset diarrhoea after hospital admission. Two-step algorithm: GDH (antigen) + toxin A/B EIA; PCR if discordant. Severity: severe = WBC >15, creatinine >133 µmol/L (or 1.5× baseline), albumin <30; fulminant = hypotension, ileus, toxic megacolon. Isolate; contact precautions; soap and water hand-washing (alcohol gel ineffective). Stop offending antibiotic where possible. Do NOT use loperamide.

outcomes.summary: Suspected CDI — test, isolate, stop offending antibiotic
outcomes.detail: Two-step GDH+toxin; severity guides treatment; no loperamide.

references.label: IDSA/SHEA Clinical Practice Guidelines for C. difficile Infection in Adults and Children 2021 focused update

title: C. difficile infection — vancomycin/fidaxomicin per IDSA 2021
description: Initial episode: oral fidaxomicin 200 mg BD × 10 days OR oral vancomycin 125 mg QDS × 10 days (preferred over metronidazole — IDSA 2021). First recurrence: fidaxomicin 200 mg BD × 10 days, or pulsed/tapered oral vancomycin. Second or further recurrence: fidaxomicin pulse/tapered, faecal microbiota transplantation, bezlotoxumab (anti-toxin B mAb) as adjunct in high-risk recurrence. Fulminant CDI: IV metronidazole 500 mg every 8 h plus oral vancomycin 500 mg QDS (rectal vanco enema if ileus). Early surgical review for toxic megacolon.

outcomes.summary: CDI initial episode — fidaxomicin or oral vancomycin
outcomes.detail: Metronidazole no longer first-line; FMT for recurrent disease; surgery for fulminant.

references.label: IDSA/SHEA 2021 focused update

title: Catheter-related bloodstream infection — remove device + targeted therapy
description: Diagnose CRBSI by paired blood cultures (peripheral and through line, line cultures positive >2 h earlier or differential bacterial colony count >3:1). Remove the catheter where possible — required for S. aureus, Pseudomonas, Candida, tunnel infection, persistent positive blood cultures despite 72 h treatment, sepsis. Tunnelled or long-term catheter can be salvaged with antibiotic lock therapy plus systemic antibiotics for coagulase-negative staphylococci or enterococci. Empirical antibiotics: vancomycin (MRSA) ± gram-negative cover (cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam) tailored to local epidemiology. Echocardiogram for S. aureus bacteraemia.

outcomes.summary: CRBSI — remove line for S. aureus/Pseudomonas/Candida/sepsis
outcomes.detail: Empirical vanco ± gram-negative; echo for S. aureus bacteraemia.

references.label: IDSA Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Intravascular Catheter-Related Infection 2009

codings.display: Bloodstream infection due to central venous catheter

title: Surgical antibiotic prophylaxis — single dose within 60 min
description: Administer surgical antibiotic prophylaxis within 60 minutes before knife-to-skin (within 120 min for vancomycin and fluoroquinolones — slow infusion). Single dose covers most procedures. Re-dose intra-operatively for prolonged procedures (>4 h or two half-lives), major blood loss (>1.5 L). Do NOT extend prophylaxis postoperatively for routine procedures — no benefit and drives resistance and CDI. Choose narrow-spectrum agent per procedure (cefuroxime, co-amoxiclav, gentamicin); MRSA-targeted (vancomycin) only for documented colonisation.

outcomes.summary: Surgical prophylaxis — single dose ≤60 min pre-incision
outcomes.detail: Re-dose intraoperatively for prolonged surgery or blood loss; no postoperative extension.

references.label: NICE NG125 Surgical site infections 2019

title: Latent TB infection — shorter regimens (3HP, 4R, 6H)
description: Treat latent TB infection in: HIV, recent contacts of pulmonary TB, healthcare workers, immunosuppression candidates (anti-TNF, transplant), silicosis, dialysis, IGRA or TST positive with risk factors. WHO 2020 / NICE: shorter regimens preferred. 3HP (isoniazid + rifapentine weekly × 12 weeks) and 4R (rifampicin daily × 4 months) preferred over 6H (isoniazid × 6 months). Add pyridoxine 25 mg with isoniazid (peripheral neuropathy). LFT before and during; monitor for hepatotoxicity. Drug interactions with rifampicin (warfarin, contraceptives, ART). Exclude active TB first (CXR, symptoms screen).

outcomes.summary: LTBI — 3HP or 4R preferred over 6H
outcomes.detail: Exclude active TB first; pyridoxine with isoniazid; LFT monitoring.

references.label: WHO Latent TB Infection: Updated and consolidated guidelines for programmatic management 2020

title: HIV PrEP — eligibility and initiation
description: Offer HIV PrEP to people at substantial risk of HIV: MSM with condomless anal sex, recent STI (rectal gonorrhoea or syphilis), or partner with HIV not virally suppressed; serodifferent partner not on suppressive ART; transgender people at risk; people who inject drugs; selected heterosexual people. Daily oral TDF/FTC. Event-based dosing (2+1+1) for MSM. Long-acting injectable cabotegravir alternative. Before initiating: confirm HIV-negative (recent test), creatinine, hepatitis B status (HBV vaccine if non-immune, alternative agent if active HBV — withdrawal can flare HBV), STI screen. Monitor every 3 months: HIV, STI, creatinine.

outcomes.summary: HIV PrEP — offer to those at substantial risk
outcomes.detail: TDF/FTC daily or 2+1+1 MSM; cabotegravir LA alternative; quarterly monitoring.

references.label: WHO PrEP Guidelines 2022
BHIVA/BASHH PrEP Guidelines 2018

title: HIV PEP — initiate within 72 hours
description: For potential HIV exposure (sexual, occupational, IV) consider PEP if within 72 hours of exposure (ideally within 24 h). Risk-assess: source HIV status (known positive vs unknown), exposure type (receptive anal > vaginal > insertive; needle-stick variable). Regimen: TDF/FTC + raltegravir or dolutegravir for 28 days. Baseline HIV, hepatitis B/C, STI screen, pregnancy, creatinine. Follow-up HIV testing at 6 weeks (4th-gen) and 3 months (definitive). PrEP counselling for ongoing exposures.

outcomes.summary: HIV exposure — PEP within 72 h, ideally <24 h
outcomes.detail: TDF/FTC + raltegravir/dolutegravir × 28 d; HIV testing at 6 w and 3 m.

references.label: BHIVA/BASHH PEP Guidelines 2021
WHO PEP for HIV Guidelines 2014 update

codings.display: Contact with and exposure to HIV

title: COVID-19 antiviral — nirmatrelvir-ritonavir within 5 days
description: Offer nirmatrelvir-ritonavir 300/100 mg BD × 5 days for non-hospitalised adults with COVID-19, symptoms ≤5 days, plus high risk for severe disease: age ≥65 (some guidance ≥50), immunocompromised, multiple comorbidities (CKD, COPD, CV disease, obesity, diabetes), Down syndrome, pregnant. Strong CYP3A4 inhibitor — check drug interactions (statins, anticoagulants, immunosuppressants, antiarrhythmics). Renal dose: eGFR 30-60 reduce to 150/100 BD; avoid eGFR <30. Alternatives: remdesivir 3-day IV course, molnupiravir (least effective, avoid in pregnancy/conception). Hospitalised severe — dexamethasone, tocilizumab/baricitinib per protocol.

outcomes.summary: High-risk COVID-19 ≤5 days symptoms — nirmatrelvir-ritonavir
outcomes.detail: Major drug interactions via CYP3A4; renal dose adjustment; alternatives if contraindicated.

references.label: WHO Therapeutics and COVID-19: Living guideline 2024
NICE TA878 Nirmatrelvir plus ritonavir for treating COVID-19 2023

title: WHO AWaRe — favour Access antibiotics
description: WHO 2024 AWaRe target ≥60% of antibiotic prescribing in the Access category (e.g. amoxicillin, ampicillin, cefalexin, cefazolin, doxycycline, gentamicin, metronidazole, nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim, sulfamethoxazole). Watch (broader-spectrum, higher resistance potential) and Reserve (last-line) use should be justified by sensitivities or specific indications. Restrict use of broad-spectrum agents (carbapenems, third-generation cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, glycopeptides) to identified need; review at 48-72 h and de-escalate to Access where possible.

outcomes.summary: AWaRe — aim ≥60% Access; justify Watch/Reserve
outcomes.detail: De-escalate to Access at 48-72 h; reserve broad-spectrum for documented need.

references.label: WHO AWaRe Antibiotic Book 2022

title: MRSA carriage — decolonisation regimen
description: Offer MRSA decolonisation in: pre-surgery (cardiothoracic, orthopaedic implants), recurrent MRSA skin infections, household clusters, ICU/haematology on admission. Regimen: mupirocin 2% nasal ointment TDS × 5 days plus chlorhexidine 4% body wash daily × 5 days; treat household contacts simultaneously where appropriate. Avoid prolonged repeated courses (mupirocin resistance). Pre-operative screening swabs (nose, throat, perineum, wounds) 1-2 weeks before surgery.

outcomes.summary: MRSA carriage pre-op or recurrent — mupirocin + chlorhexidine × 5 d
outcomes.detail: Avoid prolonged repeated courses; screen 1-2 weeks before surgery.

references.label: NICE NG125 Surgical site infections 2019

title: Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis — indications
description: Offer PJP prophylaxis to: HIV with CD4 <200 cells/μL or oral candidiasis or AIDS-defining illness, until CD4 sustained >200 for ≥3 months on ART; solid-organ transplant for 6-12 months; haematological malignancy with intensive chemo (e.g. ALL induction); high-dose steroids ≥20 mg prednisolone equivalent for ≥4 weeks. First-line: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 480 mg daily (or 960 mg three times weekly). Alternatives: dapsone 100 mg daily (test G6PD), atovaquone 1500 mg daily, nebulised pentamidine 300 mg monthly. Adjust per renal function.

outcomes.summary: PJP prophylaxis — co-trimoxazole 480 mg/d in eligible immunosuppressed
outcomes.detail: Alternatives: dapsone (after G6PD), atovaquone, pentamidine.

references.label: BHIVA Opportunistic Infection Guidelines 2022
EBMT/ECIL guidelines for PJP prophylaxis 2016

title: Asplenia/hyposplenism — vaccines and antibiotic prophylaxis
description: For asplenia (functional or anatomic) — vaccinate against encapsulated organisms: pneumococcal (PCV13 then PPV23 8 weeks later, PPV23 5-yearly), meningococcal ACWY and B, Hib (single dose), annual influenza. Ideally 2 weeks before splenectomy; otherwise 2 weeks after. Lifelong antibiotic prophylaxis (phenoxymethylpenicillin 250-500 mg BD or erythromycin if penicillin allergic) for first 1-3 years and longer for high-risk groups (children <16, immunocompromised, previous serious pneumococcal infection). Provide emergency antibiotic supply for febrile illness; medic-alert; travel advice; malaria prophylaxis vigilance.

outcomes.summary: Asplenia — vaccinate + lifetime antibiotic prophylaxis high-risk
outcomes.detail: PCV13 + PPV23 + MenACWY + MenB + Hib + flu yearly; emergency Abx supply and medic-alert.

references.label: BSH Guidelines for the prevention and treatment of infection in patients with an absent or dysfunctional spleen 2011

title: Sepsis — source control within 6-12 hours
description: Identify and control the source of sepsis as early as possible — within 6-12 hours of recognition where feasible. Examples: drain abscesses (percutaneous or surgical), debride infected tissue (necrotising fasciitis emergency), remove infected devices (lines, prosthetics), relieve obstructed urinary or biliary system. Delay in source control is independently associated with mortality. Coordinate radiology and surgery; do not wait for antibiotics to "work" before considering source.

outcomes.summary: Sepsis — source control within 6-12 hours
outcomes.detail: Drain, debride, remove devices, relieve obstruction; do not wait for antibiotics alone.

references.label: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021

title: Fluoroquinolones — restricted use due to disabling adverse effects
description: MHRA / EMA restrictions: fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, ofloxacin) should NOT be used for mild to moderate, self-limiting, or non-bacterial infections (e.g. uncomplicated UTI in many guidelines, sore throat, simple bronchitis). Reserve for serious infections only. Risks: tendinopathy and rupture (especially Achilles), aortic aneurysm/dissection, peripheral neuropathy, prolonged QT, CNS effects (anxiety, psychosis, suicidal ideation), hypoglycaemia, hyperglycaemia, retinal detachment. Avoid in age >60, steroid use, prior tendon disorder, aneurysm history, organ transplant.

outcomes.summary: Fluoroquinolones — restricted use; do not use for self-limiting infection
outcomes.detail: Tendon rupture, aortic dissection, neuropathy, QT prolongation — counsel and avoid in high-risk.

references.label: MHRA Fluoroquinolone antibiotics: must now only be prescribed when other commonly recommended antibiotics are inappropriate 2024

title: Infective endocarditis prophylaxis — restricted indications
description: NICE: do NOT routinely offer antibiotic prophylaxis for dental and non-dental procedures in adults at risk of IE. Consider antibiotic prophylaxis for highest-risk patients undergoing a dental procedure with manipulation of gingival/periapical region: prosthetic valve (including TAVI), previous IE, congenital heart disease with shunt or after repair within 6 months, residual defect after repair, heart transplant with cardiac valvulopathy. Amoxicillin 3 g PO 60 min before; clindamycin 600 mg if penicillin-allergic.

outcomes.summary: IE prophylaxis — only for highest-risk + dental manipulation
outcomes.detail: Routine prophylaxis not recommended; specialist input for borderline cases.

references.label: NICE CG64 Prophylaxis against infective endocarditis 2008 (updated 2016)
ESC IE Guidelines 2023

codings.display: Encounter for surveillance of antibiotic therapy

title: ESBL-producing Enterobacterales — carbapenem-sparing strategy
description: For UTI caused by ESBL-producing organism: nitrofurantoin or fosfomycin for cystitis (if susceptible). For non-severe bacteraemia with susceptible organism: piperacillin-tazobactam non-inferior in selected cases (MERINO context-dependent — favours meropenem for severe bacteraemia or BSI from non-urinary source). Carbapenem (meropenem or ertapenem) for severe infection or high source. Avoid amoxicillin-clavulanate alone for severe systemic infection with ESBL. Use cultures and source to guide. Consider new options (ceftolozane-tazobactam, ceftazidime-avibactam) for difficult-to-treat resistant gram-negatives per local stewardship.

outcomes.summary: ESBL — nitrofurantoin/fosfomycin for cystitis; carbapenem for severe
outcomes.detail: Piperacillin-tazobactam non-inferior for selected non-severe; new agents per stewardship.

references.label: IDSA Guidance on the Treatment of Antimicrobial-Resistant Gram-Negative Infections 2024

codings.display: Resistance to unspecified beta lactam antibiotics

title: MDR-TB — BPaLM 6-month all-oral regimen
description: WHO 2022 BPaLM regimen for rifampicin-resistant or MDR-TB: bedaquiline + pretomanid + linezolid + moxifloxacin for 6 months — high cure rate, all-oral, shortened from 9-18 months. Indications: rifampicin-resistant TB confirmed (or strong suspicion in MDR-TB epidemic setting), no extensive disease, no quinolone resistance. Monitor: ECG (QT prolongation — bedaquiline, moxifloxacin), liver enzymes, FBC (linezolid myelosuppression), peripheral neuropathy. Stop linezolid at 2 months if toxicity. Decentralised care possible. Pregnancy: limited safety data — specialist input.

outcomes.summary: MDR-TB — 6-month all-oral BPaLM regimen
outcomes.detail: Monitor QT, LFT, FBC, neuropathy; bedaquiline + pretomanid + linezolid + moxifloxacin.

references.label: WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis. Module 4: Treatment - Drug-resistant TB 2022 update

title: Procalcitonin — guiding antibiotic duration in lower respiratory infection
description: Procalcitonin (PCT) testing can support antibiotic stewardship in lower respiratory tract infections in adult ICU and selected ED settings. PCT <0.25 ng/mL — discourage starting antibiotics; PCT >0.5 — encourage. Daily PCT trends can support antibiotic stopping (drop >80% from peak or absolute value <0.25). Do NOT use PCT in isolation; combine with clinical context, source, severity. Less useful in localised infections, immunosuppression, surgery (false elevation early), renal failure.

outcomes.summary: PCT can guide LRTI antibiotic decisions in selected settings
outcomes.detail: Do not use in isolation; ineffective in localised infection or immunosuppression.

references.label: NICE DG18 Procalcitonin testing 2015
Schuetz P et al. PCT-guided algorithms in respiratory infections. Lancet ID 2018

title: Doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis (DoxyPEP)
description: Offer doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis 200 mg PO within 72 hours after condomless sex to MSM and transgender women with recent bacterial STI or substantial ongoing exposure risk. Reduces chlamydia and syphilis by ~70%, gonorrhoea inconsistent (high tetracycline resistance regionally). Not currently recommended for cisgender women based on available trial data (ACSAP showed no effect). Monitor for STIs every 3 months; counsel re photosensitivity, GI upset, oesophageal irritation. Not a replacement for condoms, vaccination (HPV, mpox, MenACWY), PrEP.

outcomes.summary: DoxyPEP — 200 mg within 72 h post condomless sex for MSM/TGW
outcomes.detail: Not in cisgender women per current evidence; quarterly STI screen; adjunct to other prevention.

references.label: CDC Clinical Guidelines on the Use of Doxycycline Postexposure Prophylaxis for Bacterial Sexually Transmitted Infection Prevention 2024

codings.display: Encounter for other specified prophylactic measures

title: Documented antibiotic allergy — structured history at every encounter
description: At every encounter requiring antibiotic prescribing, take a structured allergy history: agent, formulation, onset (immediate <1 h or delayed), reaction (rash type, anaphylaxis features, organ involvement), action taken, tolerated alternatives since. Categorise as immediate-likely IgE-mediated, severe cutaneous adverse reaction (SJS/TEN/DRESS), benign childhood rash, or unknown. Document clearly. Refer for delabelling where appropriate. Beta-lactam cross-reactivity overestimated — true cross-reactivity between penicillins and 3rd-generation cephalosporins is <2%; minimal with carbapenems.

outcomes.summary: Document and review every "allergy" — most are not true allergies
outcomes.detail: Penicillin-cephalosporin cross-reactivity <2%; refer for delabelling where appropriate.

references.label: BSACI guidelines for the management of suspected drug allergy 2024

title: Polypharmacy review — STOPP/START criteria
description: Review medications in older patients (≥65, especially ≥75 or frail) using STOPP/START Version 3 (2023). STOPP highlights potentially inappropriate prescriptions: long-acting benzodiazepines, anticholinergics with cognitive impairment, NSAIDs in HF/CKD, duplicate drug classes, PPI beyond justified indication, indicated treatment omissions. START highlights omitted indicated treatments: anticoagulation in AF, statin for established CVD, ACEi in HFrEF, bisphosphonate in osteoporosis. Document indication, intended duration, and review date for every medicine. Engage shared decision-making with patient and carers.

outcomes.summary: Polypharmacy — apply STOPP/START at annual review
outcomes.detail: Document indication and review date for every medication; deprescribe where appropriate.

references.label: O'Mahony D et al. STOPP/START criteria for potentially inappropriate prescribing in older people v3 2023

title: Falls — multifactorial risk assessment in older adults
description: Older adult ≥65 with a fall, frequent falls, or balance/gait problems — offer multifactorial falls risk assessment: history of falls (number, mechanism, injury, syncope), medication review (psychotropics, anticholinergics, antihypertensives, hypoglycaemics — STOPPFall), gait and balance (Timed Up and Go ≥12 s; Berg Balance; Tinetti), vision, footwear, postural BP, ECG, cognitive screen, bone health (DEXA, FRAX), home hazards, alcohol. Tailored intervention: strength and balance training, medication reduction, vitamin D if deficient (NOT routine high-dose), bone protection, home modification, ophthalmology, cataract surgery.

outcomes.summary: Falls in older adult — multifactorial assessment + intervention
outcomes.detail: Strength/balance training, medication review, home safety, vision, bone health.

references.label: NICE CG161 Falls in older people 2013 (updated 2024)
World guidelines for falls prevention and management for older adults 2022

title: Frailty — Clinical Frailty Scale and advance care planning
description: Identify frailty using Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale (1-9) at admission and in primary care. CFS ≥5 — mild frailty; ≥6 moderate; ≥7 severe; ≥8 very severe; 9 terminally ill. Trigger comprehensive geriatric assessment. Initiate advance care planning: discuss preferences for ceiling of care, resuscitation, hospitalisation, place of care, treatment escalation; document via ReSPECT or equivalent. Review at change of state. CFS ≥7 has prognostic significance for mortality and outcomes from critical illness, surgery, and intensive treatments.

outcomes.summary: CFS ≥5 — frailty; engage in ACP and CGA
outcomes.detail: CFS ≥7 has clear prognostic implications; document treatment escalation plans.

references.label: Rockwood K et al. A global clinical measure of fitness and frailty. CMAJ 2005
BGS Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment 2014

title: Delirium — 4AT and CAM screening
description: Screen for delirium with 4AT (4 items, ≥4 minutes): alertness, AMT4, attention (months backward), acute change/fluctuating course. Score ≥4 indicates possible delirium. CAM-ICU for ventilated/intubated patients. Identify precipitants (TIME-IT): trauma, infection, metabolic, environment, medications, intracranial, toxic. Treat the cause. Non-pharmacological first — reorientation, hearing/vision aids, hydration, mobilisation, sleep, family presence, familiar objects. Avoid restraints. Antipsychotic (haloperidol 0.5-1 mg or olanzapine 2.5 mg) only for severe agitation endangering self or staff; lowest dose, shortest time; avoid in Lewy body dementia/Parkinson's (use lorazepam instead).

outcomes.summary: Delirium — 4AT/CAM screen; treat cause; non-pharmacological first
outcomes.detail: Antipsychotic only for severe agitation; avoid in DLB/PD.

references.label: NICE CG103 Delirium: prevention, diagnosis and management 2010 (updated 2023)

codings.display: Delirium due to known physiological condition

title: Anticholinergic burden — review in cognitive impairment
description: Calculate anticholinergic burden using Anticholinergic Cognitive Burden scale (ACB) or Anticholinergic Drug Scale (ADS). Total ACB ≥3 associated with cognitive decline, dementia, falls, hospitalisation, and mortality in older adults. Common offenders: tricyclic antidepressants, paroxetine, oxybutynin/tolterodine, hyoscine, promethazine, chlorpheniramine, hydroxyzine, low-potency antipsychotics (chlorpromazine, olanzapine), prochlorperazine. Replace with non-anticholinergic alternatives where possible (e.g. mirabegron for overactive bladder, cetirizine for allergy, sertraline for depression).

outcomes.summary: ACB ≥3 — review and reduce anticholinergic burden
outcomes.detail: Substitute alternatives where possible; effect cumulative across drugs.

references.label: Coupland CAC et al. Anticholinergic drug exposure and the risk of dementia. JAMA Intern Med 2019

title: Pressure injury — Braden scale risk and SSKIN bundle
description: Use Braden scale on admission and at risk-change: sensory perception, moisture, activity, mobility, nutrition, friction/shear. Score ≤18 indicates at-risk (≤12 high risk). Implement SSKIN bundle: Surface (high-specification mattress and cushion), Skin inspection daily, Keep moving (repositioning 2-4 hourly), Incontinence/moisture management, Nutrition (assess MUST, treat). Document positioning and skin findings. Stage existing injuries by EPUAP: 1 (non-blanching erythema), 2 (partial thickness), 3 (full thickness), 4 (down to bone/muscle), unstageable, deep tissue injury.

outcomes.summary: Braden ≤18 — apply SSKIN bundle and reposition
outcomes.detail: High-specification surfaces; nutrition; document staging by EPUAP.

references.label: EPUAP/NPIAP/PPPIA International Guideline 2019
NICE CG179 Pressure ulcers: prevention and management 2014 (updated)

codings.display: Pressure ulcer of unspecified site, unspecified stage

title: Constipation in older adults — laxative ladder
description: Stepwise approach to constipation: lifestyle (fluid, fibre, mobility) + identify causes (drugs, dehydration, hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia, depression). Bulk laxative (ispaghula, methylcellulose) — only if adequate fluid intake. Osmotic (macrogol/polyethylene glycol first-line; lactulose second). Stimulant (senna, bisacodyl) if no response — short-term to avoid melanosis coli. Combine osmotic + stimulant for opioid-induced constipation. Newer agents (naloxegol, methylnaltrexone) for opioid-induced refractory. Avoid prolonged stimulant or routine enema. Manual disimpaction for severe faecal impaction.

outcomes.summary: Constipation — macrogol first; combine with stimulant for opioid-induced
outcomes.detail: Address drug causes; bulk laxatives require fluid; specific agents for opioid-induced.

references.label: NICE CKS Constipation 2024

title: Drug-induced hyponatraemia — common offenders
description: Review medications in any hyponatraemia (Na <135 mmol/L), particularly in older adults. Common drug causes: SSRIs (especially in first 4 weeks), thiazides (within 2 weeks of initiation), carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, valproate, antipsychotics, PPIs, MDMA. Mechanism varies (SIADH, hypovolaemia). Step 1 — stop or replace offending agent. Step 2 — investigate cause (volume status, serum/urine osmolality, urine sodium, TSH, cortisol). Step 3 — treat by mechanism (fluid restriction for SIADH, volume repletion for hypovolaemia). See "hyponatraemia correction limits" for severe/symptomatic management.

outcomes.summary: Hyponatraemia — review drug history (SSRI/thiazide/AED/PPI)
outcomes.detail: Stop or substitute offending agent; investigate cause; correct slowly.

references.label: European Society of Endocrinology Hyponatraemia 2014

title: Statin in older adults — continue vs deprescribe
description: For older adults already on statin for secondary prevention — continue unless intolerance, adverse effects, or life expectancy <1 year. For primary prevention in age ≥75 with no established CVD — limited trial data; consider individual benefit, expected life expectancy, polypharmacy, frailty (CFS), and patient preference (STAREE ongoing). Statins remain net beneficial in most secondary prevention regardless of age. Deprescribing trial (3-6 months) reasonable in frail older patients on primary prevention or with limited life expectancy.

outcomes.summary: Statin in elderly — continue secondary; individualise primary
outcomes.detail: Frailty and life expectancy guide decisions; deprescribing trial reasonable in primary prevention.

references.label: NICE CG181 (updated)

title: DOAC in elderly with falls and AF — continue per ESC
description: Older patient with AF and falls or perceived fall risk should generally continue oral anticoagulation if CHA2DS2-VASc indicates net benefit — risk of stroke without OAC vastly outweighs risk of intracranial haemorrhage from falls (a patient needs >295 falls per year for fall-related ICH to outweigh stroke risk per Man-Son-Hing model). Optimise modifiable bleed risk (BP, alcohol, NSAIDs); HAS-BLED is for risk identification, not a reason to withhold OAC. Consider apixaban (lowest bleed in elderly per ARISTOTLE). Address fall causes; assess frailty; involve patient and family in shared decision.

outcomes.summary: AF + falls — continue OAC; apixaban preferred in elderly
outcomes.detail: Address fall causes, modifiable bleed risks; HAS-BLED not a stop signal.
