references.label: ESC AF Guidelines 2024
Man-Son-Hing M et al. JAMA 1999

title: Dementia BPSD — non-pharmacological first
description: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (agitation, aggression, wandering, psychosis, depression). Step 1: identify and treat reversible cause — pain, infection, constipation, urinary retention, dehydration, sensory deprivation, depression, environmental factors. Step 2: non-pharmacological — structured routine, exercise, music therapy, social interaction, family involvement, environmental modification. Step 3: pharmacotherapy ONLY if severe distress or risk to self/others. Risperidone (off-label in UK, licensed short-term — max 6 weeks) for severe aggression/psychosis; quetiapine for Lewy body/Parkinson's dementia. AVOID benzodiazepines (paradoxical agitation, falls). Reduce/discontinue at 6-12 weeks.

outcomes.summary: BPSD — identify reversible cause; non-pharm first; risperidone short-term only
outcomes.detail: Avoid benzodiazepines; review antipsychotic at 6-12 weeks with view to stopping.

references.label: NICE NG97 Dementia: assessment, management and support 2018

title: Cognitive assessment — MoCA, Mini-Cog, GPCOG
description: Use validated cognitive screening tools: Mini-Cog (3-min screen, 3-word recall + clock draw), MoCA (10 min, more sensitive for mild cognitive impairment), GPCOG (primary care). Adjust for educational level and language. Positive screen — refer to memory clinic; secondary investigations: blood tests (FBC, U&E, LFT, glucose, TSH, B12, folate, calcium, Mg), MRI brain (volumetric for hippocampus), and specialist evaluation (neuropsychology, occasionally CSF biomarkers or amyloid PET in specialist context). Counsel patient and family; consider driving, finances, advance planning.

outcomes.summary: Suspected cognitive impairment — MoCA/Mini-Cog screen, memory clinic referral
outcomes.detail: Investigate reversible causes; specialist evaluation for diagnosis.

references.label: NICE NG97 Dementia 2018

title: Vitamin D supplementation in older adults
description: Offer vitamin D 800-2000 IU daily (or 10 mcg + dietary advice) to: adults ≥65, housebound, dark skin or covered, autumn-winter in northern latitudes, history of osteoporotic fracture, on bone-active medication. Routine high-dose loading not needed unless markedly deficient (25-OH vitamin D <25 nmol/L). Calcium intake from diet preferred over supplements unless inadequate intake; if supplementation needed, modest doses (500-1000 mg) divided to minimise CV concerns. Test 25-OH vitamin D only when deficiency-related disease suspected, not for screening.

outcomes.summary: Older adults — vitamin D 800-2000 IU/day; calcium from diet preferred
outcomes.detail: Test only when clinically indicated; modest calcium supplements if needed.

references.label: NICE PH56 Vitamin D 2014 (updated)
ROS Vitamin D and bone health: a practical clinical guideline 2018

title: Bisphosphonate drug holiday — reassess at 5 years
description: After 3-5 years of oral bisphosphonate or 3 years of IV zoledronate consider a drug holiday — reassessment of fracture risk: continue if T-score remains <-2.5 at hip, prior vertebral or hip fracture, or new fragility fracture on treatment. Holiday for 1-3 years with monitoring (DEXA every 1-2 years). Drug holiday reduces risk of rare adverse effects — atypical femoral fractures (incidence increases with duration >3-5 years) and osteonecrosis of the jaw. Reassess for resumption or switch to denosumab/teriparatide. Denosumab does NOT have a drug holiday — withdrawal causes rebound vertebral fractures.

outcomes.summary: Bisphosphonate at 3-5 years — reassess for holiday
outcomes.detail: Continue if high risk persists; holiday reduces AFF and ONJ risk; denosumab requires no holiday.

references.label: NICE TA464 Bisphosphonates 2017

title: Sarcopenia and undernutrition — MUST and SARC-F screening
description: Screen older adults for nutritional risk with MUST (Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool): BMI <20 (or recent unplanned weight loss ≥5%), and acute illness affecting intake; score ≥2 high risk. Screen for sarcopenia with SARC-F (strength, assistance walking, rise from chair, climb stairs, falls — ≥4 positive). Confirm sarcopenia with low muscle strength (grip), low muscle mass (DEXA/BIA), low physical performance (gait speed). Manage: protein intake 1.0-1.2 g/kg/day (1.2-1.5 if illness), resistance exercise, vitamin D, treat underlying conditions. Refer dietitian.

outcomes.summary: Older adults — MUST + SARC-F screening
outcomes.detail: Resistance exercise + protein 1.0-1.5 g/kg/day; dietitian referral.

references.label: EWGSOP2 Sarcopenia consensus 2019
BAPEN MUST screening tool

title: End of life — five priorities of care
description: When death is imminent: (1) recognise — possibility of dying considered, communicated openly; (2) communicate sensitively with patient and family; (3) involve patient in decisions; (4) support family and those important; (5) individualised plan including symptom management (anticipatory medicines for pain, secretions, agitation, dyspnoea, nausea), spiritual/cultural needs, place of death preferences. Avoid futile investigations and interventions. Document via locally adopted tools (ReSPECT). Bereavement support for family.

outcomes.summary: EoL — recognise, communicate, involve, support, individualise
outcomes.detail: Anticipatory medicines; respect preferences; family and spiritual support.

references.label: Leadership Alliance for the Care of Dying People One chance to get it right 2014
NICE NG31 Care of dying adults in the last days of life 2015

title: Urinary incontinence in older adults — TIPS and treatment
description: Assess type: stress, urge, mixed, overflow (chronic retention), functional. Causes (DIAPERS mnemonic): Delirium, Infection, Atrophic urethritis, Pharmacological (diuretics, sedatives, anticholinergics), Excess urine output (diabetes, CHF, hypercalcaemia), Restricted mobility, Stool impaction. Conservative: bladder training, pelvic floor exercises, fluid timing, treat constipation, weight loss. Pharmacological: anticholinergic (oxybutynin, solifenacin) for overactive bladder — caution in cognitive impairment, use mirabegron alternative; topical oestrogen for postmenopausal women. Refer urology/uro-gynae if conservative fails.

outcomes.summary: UI in elderly — assess type and reversible causes (DIAPERS); avoid anticholinergic in cognitive impairment
outcomes.detail: Mirabegron alternative for OAB; topical oestrogen for GSM; conservative first.

references.label: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence 2019

title: Suicidality — C-SSRS screening and risk stratification
description: Use Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale to screen and stratify. Active ideation with method/plan/intent — high acute risk, ensure safe environment, urgent mental health assessment, do not leave alone, remove access to means (firearms, medications, ligature points). Passive ideation or ideation without plan — moderate risk, safety plan, social support, follow-up within 24-72 h. Past attempt is the strongest predictor of future suicide. Treat the underlying condition (depression, psychosis, substance use); psychological interventions, pharmacotherapy. Lethal means counselling and safe-storage education.

outcomes.summary: Active suicidal ideation with plan/intent — same-day MH assessment + remove means
outcomes.detail: Past attempt is strongest predictor; safety plan and follow-up; lethal-means counselling.

references.label: Posner K et al. Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS). Am J Psychiatry 2011

title: Acute agitation — de-escalation first, rapid tranquillisation as last resort
description: Acute behavioural disturbance: de-escalation first (calm environment, low stimulation, address basic needs, listen, set limits). If escalation despite de-escalation and risk to self or others: offer oral medication first (lorazepam 1-2 mg or olanzapine 10 mg or promethazine 25-50 mg, repeated). IM as last resort: lorazepam 1-2 mg IM, or olanzapine 10 mg IM (NOT within 1 h of IM benzodiazepine — respiratory depression), or haloperidol 5 mg + promethazine 25-50 mg IM. Monitor: SpO2, RR, BP, HR, level of consciousness, ECG (QT, especially haloperidol), temperature. Have flumazenil available.

outcomes.summary: Acute agitation — de-escalation first; oral RT before IM
outcomes.detail: Avoid olanzapine + benzo IM within 1 h; monitor RR/SpO2/QT.

references.label: NICE NG10 Violence and aggression: short-term management in mental health 2015

title: Acute mania — first-line antipsychotic + mood stabiliser
description: For acute mania start an antipsychotic (olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine, haloperidol, aripiprazole) for rapid symptom control. Add or switch to a mood stabiliser (lithium or valproate) for recurrence prevention — choice influenced by previous response, comorbidities, and reproductive potential. Lithium first-line for long-term mood stabilisation; avoid valproate in women of childbearing potential (Pregnancy Prevention Programme). Sedation (benzodiazepines short-term). Suspend antidepressants. Consider ECT for severe/treatment-resistant mania. Hospitalise if risk to self/others, severe loss of insight, or vulnerable.

outcomes.summary: Acute mania — antipsychotic + lithium/valproate; avoid valproate in women of childbearing potential
outcomes.detail: Suspend antidepressants; consider ECT for severe; hospitalise if high risk.

references.label: NICE CG185 Bipolar disorder 2014 (updated 2023)

codings.display: Manic episode without psychotic symptoms, unspecified

title: First-episode psychosis — early intervention service + atypical antipsychotic
description: Refer all first-episode psychosis to Early Intervention in Psychosis service within 2 weeks. Offer an atypical antipsychotic (aripiprazole, risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, paliperidone) plus CBT for psychosis (CBTp) plus family intervention. Monitor weight, lipids, glucose, prolactin, ECG (QT), movement disorders. Long-acting injectable (LAI) considered early to support adherence. Continue antipsychotic for at least 1-2 years after symptom resolution. Clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (failure of ≥2 antipsychotics including one atypical) — register with monitoring service; haematological monitoring.

outcomes.summary: FEP — EIP referral within 2 weeks; atypical antipsychotic + CBTp
outcomes.detail: LAI early for adherence; clozapine for treatment-resistant; metabolic and movement monitoring.

references.label: NICE CG178 Psychosis and schizophrenia in adults 2014 (updated)

title: ADHD — NICE NG87 assessment pathway
description: Refer for specialist assessment (psychiatry, paediatrics, or appropriate specialist) where ADHD suspected and symptoms cause significant impairment across more than one setting. Diagnosis requires DSM-5/ICD-11 criteria, symptoms before age 12, persistent ≥6 months, multiple settings. First-line pharmacotherapy in children ≥5: methylphenidate (immediate or modified release); in adults: methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine. Atomoxetine and guanfacine alternatives. Monitor cardiovascular (BP, HR), growth in children, mental state. Combine with parent-training programmes for under-5s (medication only after specialist assessment in <5), CBT, environmental adaptations.

outcomes.summary: Suspected ADHD — specialist referral; multimodal management
outcomes.detail: Stimulants first-line in school-age and adults; cardiovascular monitoring.

references.label: NICE NG87 ADHD: diagnosis and management 2018 (updated 2019)

title: Eating disorder — medical instability (MEED/MARSIPAN)
description: Use MEED criteria to identify medical risk: very high risk — BMI <13 (adult) or <70% median BMI (child), heart rate <40, postural drop systolic >20 or HR rise >35, K+ <3.0, Na <130, phosphate <0.5, glucose <2.5, ECG abnormalities (long QT, U waves). High risk — admit acute medical with eating disorder team input. Refeeding syndrome risk: start nutrition cautiously (5-10 kcal/kg/day in highest risk), check and replace phosphate, magnesium, potassium, thiamine BEFORE refeeding, monitor daily electrolytes for first week. Compassionate, multidisciplinary care; psychological treatment integral.

outcomes.summary: ED with medical instability — MEED very-high risk: admit medical
outcomes.detail: Refeeding syndrome risk — cautious initiation, daily electrolytes, thiamine.

references.label: Royal College of Psychiatrists MEED Medical Emergencies in Eating Disorders 2022

title: PTSD — trauma-focused CBT or EMDR first-line
description: Offer trauma-focused CBT (TF-CBT) or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR) as first-line for PTSD; both are evidence-based. Pharmacotherapy second-line or where psychological therapy not accepted/effective — SSRI (sertraline, paroxetine) or venlafaxine. Avoid benzodiazepines (worsen PTSD outcomes, dependence). Consider prazosin for trauma-related nightmares (mixed evidence per AHEAD trial). Address comorbidities (depression, substance misuse, suicidality). Specialist trauma services for complex PTSD or refractory cases. Screening tool: PCL-5 or short form.

outcomes.summary: PTSD — TF-CBT or EMDR first; avoid benzodiazepines
outcomes.detail: SSRI/venlafaxine pharmacotherapy; prazosin for nightmares (mixed evidence).

references.label: NICE NG116 Post-traumatic stress disorder 2018

title: Generalised anxiety disorder — stepped care
description: Step 1 — identification, education, active monitoring. Step 2 — low-intensity psychological intervention (CBT-based self-help, psychoeducational groups). Step 3 — high-intensity psychological intervention (CBT or applied relaxation) OR pharmacotherapy. First-line drug: SSRI (sertraline). Alternatives: SNRI (duloxetine, venlafaxine), pregabalin (if SSRI/SNRI intolerant or ineffective). Avoid benzodiazepines beyond 2-4 weeks (dependence). Step 4 — refer specialist mental health for refractory or complex cases. Combine pharmacotherapy with psychological therapy where possible.

outcomes.summary: GAD — stepped care; SSRI/SNRI first-line; avoid prolonged benzos
outcomes.detail: Pregabalin alternative; combine with psychological therapy.

references.label: NICE CG113 Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder 2011 (updated)

title: OCD — CBT with exposure and response prevention
description: First-line for OCD: CBT with exposure and response prevention (ERP). For moderate-severe symptoms add SSRI (any: sertraline, fluoxetine, paroxetine, fluvoxamine, citalopram, escitalopram) at the higher end of dose range and continue 12 months after remission. Clomipramine (TCA) second-line if SSRI intolerant or ineffective. Refractory: refer specialist, consider augmentation with antipsychotic (risperidone, aripiprazole), or other strategies. Monitor for harm OCD with intrusive violent or sexual thoughts — distinguish from psychosis; reassure these are typical of OCD and do not predict action.

outcomes.summary: OCD — CBT with ERP + high-dose SSRI ≥12 months
outcomes.detail: Clomipramine alternative; antipsychotic augmentation for refractory; harm OCD distinct from psychosis.

references.label: NICE CG31 Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder 2005

title: Substance use disorder — integrated care with comorbid mental health
description: Coexisting mental health and substance use disorder ("dual diagnosis") is common and requires integrated, simultaneous treatment — not sequential. Single-team approach where possible. Screen all mental health presentations for substance use (AUDIT, DUDIT) and all substance use presentations for mental health (PHQ-9, GAD-7, C-SSRS). Treat both; pharmacotherapy and psychosocial. Harm reduction (clean needles, naloxone, safer-use education). Address social determinants — housing, employment, relationships. Engage family/carers where appropriate. Long-term follow-up and assertive engagement.

outcomes.summary: Dual diagnosis — integrated simultaneous treatment
outcomes.detail: Screen both directions; harm reduction; long-term engagement.

references.label: NICE NG58 Coexisting severe mental illness and substance misuse 2016

title: Lithium — monitoring and toxicity prevention
description: Before starting lithium: U&E, eGFR, TFT, calcium, FBC, ECG, pregnancy. Therapeutic range typically 0.6-0.8 mmol/L (target 0.8-1.0 mmol/L in acute mania, lower 0.4-0.6 in elderly/maintenance). Check level every week until stable, then every 3-6 months. Level 12 hours post-dose. Annual: U&E, calcium, TFT, weight. Toxicity warning signs: tremor (coarse), ataxia, confusion, vomiting, polyuria, hyperreflexia, seizure. Triggers: dehydration, NSAID/ACEi/diuretic addition, infection, renal impairment, low-sodium diet. Levels >1.5 mmol/L symptomatic — admit; >2.0 — severe toxicity, consider haemodialysis. Educate patient about hydration, NSAIDs, sick-day plan.

outcomes.summary: Lithium — level every 3-6 months; annual U&E/TFT/Ca; educate about toxicity
outcomes.detail: NSAIDs/ACEi/diuretics raise levels; hydration critical; level >1.5 — admit.

references.label: NICE CG185 Bipolar disorder 2014 (updated 2023)

title: Clozapine — haematological and metabolic monitoring
description: Clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia. Register with monitoring service. FBC: weekly for 18 weeks, fortnightly to 1 year, monthly thereafter. Stop clozapine and discuss with haematology if neutrophils <1.5 (or <1.0 in benign ethnic neutropenia). Monitor: weight, lipids, glucose at baseline and 3-monthly initially; ECG, troponin, CRP for myocarditis especially in first 3 months (chest pain, tachycardia, fever, flu-like — high vigilance); seizure threshold (consider AED if dose >600 mg/day); constipation (potentially fatal ileus — prophylactic laxative); sedation; sialorrhoea (hyoscine patch). Smoking cessation requires dose review (raises levels).

outcomes.summary: Clozapine — FBC monitoring, myocarditis vigilance first 3 months, constipation
outcomes.detail: Smoking cessation raises levels; prophylactic laxative; haematology referral for neutropenia.

references.label: NICE CG178 Psychosis and schizophrenia 2014
MHRA Clozapine — constipation monitoring 2017

title: Antipsychotic — metabolic and movement monitoring
description: Monitor all patients on antipsychotic medication: weight (baseline, every 12 weeks for first year, then yearly), waist circumference, BP, fasting glucose or HbA1c, lipids — annual review. Prolactin, ECG (QTc), EPSE/movement (Glasgow Antipsychotic Side-effects Scale, Simpson-Angus or Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale) at baseline and 6-monthly initially. Address modifiable cardiometabolic risk (smoking cessation, dietitian, exercise, screen-and-treat dyslipidaemia, diabetes). Switch to lower-metabolic-risk agent (aripiprazole, ziprasidone) for significant weight gain. Education on signs of NMS/tardive dyskinesia.

outcomes.summary: Antipsychotic — annual metabolic monitoring; EPSE checks
outcomes.detail: Switch agent for significant weight gain; address modifiable CV risk.

references.label: NICE CG178 Psychosis and schizophrenia 2014

title: SSRI in pregnancy — risk-benefit and neonatal monitoring
description: Untreated maternal depression is itself harmful — relapse rates after stopping SSRI in pregnancy are high. Sertraline is generally preferred SSRI in pregnancy and lactation (lowest milk transfer). Avoid paroxetine in first trimester (modest cardiac defect signal). Counsel about small but real risks: congenital cardiac defects (low absolute increase), persistent pulmonary hypertension of newborn (third trimester, absolute risk ~3/1000), poor neonatal adaptation syndrome (transient). Plan delivery in unit able to observe newborn. Continue effective antidepressant rather than stopping abruptly; specialist perinatal mental health input.

outcomes.summary: SSRI in pregnancy — sertraline preferred; do not stop abruptly
outcomes.detail: Untreated depression itself harmful; counsel small absolute risks; perinatal mental health input.

references.label: NICE CG192 Antenatal and postnatal mental health 2014 (updated 2020)

title: Autism — early identification and pathway
description: Use M-CHAT-R at 18 and 24 months in routine well-child checks; positive screen (≥3 critical items) — follow-up interview; persistent concerns — refer to specialist for ADOS-2 and DSM-5 assessment. Red flags any age: regression of language or social skills, lack of joint attention or pointing by 18 months, lack of single words by 16 months, lack of two-word phrases by 24 months, lack of eye contact, repetitive behaviours. Early intervention (Early Start Denver Model, applied behavioural analysis) before age 5 improves outcomes. Investigate co-occurring conditions: epilepsy, ID, ADHD, anxiety, sleep, GI, feeding.

outcomes.summary: M-CHAT-R at 18-24 months; refer if positive
outcomes.detail: Early intervention improves outcomes; address co-occurring conditions.

references.label: NICE CG128 Autism spectrum disorder in under 19s: recognition, referral and diagnosis 2011 (updated 2017)
Robins DL et al. M-CHAT-R/F. Pediatrics 2014

title: Self-harm — acute management and psychosocial assessment
description: Treat physical injury first (wound care, paracetamol overdose pathway, etc.). Within 4 hours of medical clearance offer a biopsychosocial assessment by mental health practitioner; do NOT discharge without it. Risk and needs assessment, safety plan, lethal-means counselling, follow-up within 7 days. Offer psychological intervention (CBT, DBT, mentalisation-based therapy, problem-solving therapy). Do not withhold treatment based on suspected manipulative motive. Avoid prescribing potentially harmful quantities of medication. Mental Capacity Act considerations.

outcomes.summary: Self-harm — psychosocial assessment within 4 h; safety plan; follow-up 7 d
outcomes.detail: No discharge without assessment; lethal-means counselling.

references.label: NICE NG225 Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence 2022

title: Gender-based violence and IPV — recognition and response
description: Routinely consider intimate partner violence in women presenting with depression, anxiety, chronic pain, GI symptoms, repeated injuries, mental health crisis, pregnancy complications. Ask in private without partner present. Empathic, non-judgmental enquiry. Document accurately for potential medico-legal use. LIVES-FW response: Listen, Inquire about needs and concerns, Validate, Enhance safety (safety plan, refuge information), Support (referrals). Do not pressure to leave or report — empower informed choices. Mandatory reporting per local law for children involved.

outcomes.summary: IPV — enquire privately, LIVES response, safety plan
outcomes.detail: Document carefully; do not pressure; mandatory reporting if children at risk.

references.label: WHO Responding to intimate partner violence and sexual violence against women: clinical and policy guidelines 2013 (updated)

title: Sexual assault — acute clinical pathway
description: Compassionate trauma-informed care. Within 7 days of assault offer: forensic examination at sexual assault referral centre (SARC) if patient wishes — preserve evidence. HIV PEP (within 72 h), hepatitis B post-exposure (vaccine ± immunoglobulin), STI prophylaxis (ceftriaxone + doxycycline + metronidazole + azithromycin per local), emergency contraception (levonorgestrel within 72 h or ulipristal within 120 h or copper IUD within 120 h). Hepatitis B vaccine if non-immune. Psychological support; written information; follow-up at 2 and 6 weeks; HIV repeat at 6 weeks and 3 months; safeguarding considerations.

outcomes.summary: Sexual assault — SARC referral, HIV PEP, EC, STI prophylaxis
outcomes.detail: HIV PEP within 72 h; EC by method per time window; psychological support.

references.label: WHO Sexual assault clinical handbook 2019
Faculty of Forensic and Legal Medicine 2024

title: Perinatal mental health — referral pathway
description: Refer to perinatal mental health service: any pregnant woman or up to 12 months postnatal with current or past serious mental illness (bipolar, schizophrenia, postpartum psychosis, severe depression with psychotic features), moderate-severe depression or anxiety, history of self-harm/suicide attempt, currently on or considering psychotropic medication. Specialist input on pre-conception counselling, medication risk-benefit through pregnancy and breastfeeding, plan for delivery and postnatal period (mother-and-baby unit if needed), prevention of postpartum psychosis in known bipolar (peri-delivery lithium).

outcomes.summary: Perinatal mental health — refer for SMI history, moderate-severe symptoms, medication review
outcomes.detail: Pre-conception planning critical for SMI; mother-and-baby unit if separation harmful.

references.label: NICE CG192 Antenatal and postnatal mental health 2014 (updated 2020)

title: PHQ-9 — depression severity, response tracking
description: Use PHQ-9 (9 items, 0-3 each, total 0-27) to grade severity: 0-4 minimal, 5-9 mild, 10-14 moderate, 15-19 moderately severe, 20-27 severe. Item 9 — any positive response to thoughts of self-harm requires same-day risk assessment. Repeat at 2 and 4 weeks after starting/changing treatment and every 4-6 weeks thereafter; aim for ≥50% reduction by 4-6 weeks (response) and PHQ-9 ≤4 (remission). Action: no response — increase dose, switch class, add psychotherapy, add second medicine; refer mental health for refractory.

outcomes.summary: PHQ-9 grades severity and tracks response
outcomes.detail: Item 9 positive — same-day risk assessment; aim ≥50% reduction by 4-6 weeks.

references.label: Kroenke K et al. PHQ-9. J Gen Intern Med 2001
NICE NG222 Depression in adults 2022

codings.display: Major depressive disorder, single episode, unspecified

title: Long COVID — initial workup and management
description: Persistent symptoms beyond 12 weeks after acute COVID-19, not explained by an alternative diagnosis. Workup: FBC, U&E, LFT, TFT, ferritin, vitamin D, glucose/HbA1c, BNP if cardiac symptoms, troponin/ECG if chest pain or palpitations, D-dimer if VTE concern, ECG, CXR, PFT if dyspnoea, echo if cardiac signs. Refer to multidisciplinary Long COVID clinic. Symptom-specific management: graded return to activity for fatigue (CAUTION: pacing, NOT graded exercise therapy if post-exertional malaise — NICE 2022), CBT for psychological symptoms, breathing pattern retraining, vestibular rehab for dizziness. Investigate orthostatic intolerance/POTS. Vaccinate. No specific disease-modifying treatment.

outcomes.summary: Long COVID — MDT clinic; pacing for PEM (not GET); symptom-specific management
outcomes.detail: Investigate orthostatic intolerance and POTS; rule out alternative diagnoses.

references.label: NICE NG188 COVID-19 rapid guideline: managing the long-term effects of COVID-19 2022 update

title: Respiratory viral testing — RSV/influenza/COVID-19 in season
description: For adult and paediatric admissions with acute respiratory infection during respiratory virus season offer multiplex PCR for RSV, influenza A/B, and SARS-CoV-2 — informs antiviral eligibility (oseltamivir for influenza, nirmatrelvir-ritonavir for COVID-19 high-risk, nirsevimab/palivizumab for at-risk infants with RSV) and infection control (cohort, side room, PPE). Surveillance data; vaccination opportunity for unvaccinated. Avoid empirical antibiotics for confirmed viral infection without bacterial features.

outcomes.summary: Acute respiratory admission in season — RSV/flu/COVID multiplex
outcomes.detail: Guides antiviral eligibility and infection control; avoid unnecessary antibiotics.

references.label: UKHSA respiratory virus surveillance 2024
WHO Guidelines for the clinical management of severe acute respiratory infection 2022

title: Mpox (monkeypox) — recognition and isolation
description: Suspect mpox in a patient with characteristic rash (vesicles, pustules, ulcers, often in genital/anal area) plus epidemiological link (recent travel to outbreak region, sexual contact with confirmed case, GBMSM with multiple partners). Isolate immediately; PPE for staff (FFP3, eye protection, gown, gloves). Notify public health. Confirm with PCR of lesion swab. Most cases self-limit; tecovirimat for severe disease, immunocompromise, paediatric, pregnant — per specialist advice. Offer post-exposure vaccination (MVA-BN) to close contacts within 4-14 days. Mpox vaccination programme for at-risk groups.

outcomes.summary: Suspected mpox — isolate, PPE, notify public health, PCR
outcomes.detail: Tecovirimat for severe/immunocompromised; post-exposure vaccination MVA-BN within 4-14 d.

references.label: WHO Clinical management and infection prevention and control for monkeypox 2022 (updated)
UKHSA mpox guidance 2024

title: Cervical screening — primary HPV testing pathway
description: England and many programmes now use primary HPV testing on cervical samples in women aged 25-64. Routine screening: 25-49 every 3 years; 50-64 every 5 years. HPV-negative — routine recall. HPV-positive but cytology normal — repeat in 12 months; persistent at 24 months — colposcopy. HPV-positive with abnormal cytology — colposcopy. HPV vaccination available for boys and girls 11-13 (catch-up to 25); single-dose now used in many programmes per WHO 2022.

outcomes.summary: Cervical screening — primary HPV testing; routine recall by age band
outcomes.detail: Persistent HPV-positive at 24 months — colposcopy; single-dose HPV vaccine programme.

references.label: NHS Cervical Screening Programme primary HPV testing guidance 2023
WHO Cervical cancer elimination initiative 2023

codings.display: Encounter for screening for malignant neoplasm of cervix

title: Bowel cancer screening — FIT and symptomatic referral
description: Offer faecal immunochemical test (FIT) as part of organised population screening (UK 50-74 every 2 years; rolling out to 50-54). FIT also used for symptomatic patients in primary care — NICE DG56 supports FIT to triage referral for unexplained symptoms (change in bowel habit, abdominal pain, anaemia). FIT ≥10 µg Hb/g → urgent 2-week referral; FIT <10 with red flag (rectal mass, abdominal mass, anal mass, unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia) → still refer. Polyps removed at colonoscopy; manage by histology and number per BSG surveillance guidelines.

outcomes.summary: Bowel symptoms — FIT first; ≥10 µg Hb/g — urgent referral
outcomes.detail: FIT does not replace red-flag clinical assessment; surveillance per BSG post-polypectomy.

references.label: NICE DG56 Quantitative faecal immunochemical tests to guide colorectal cancer pathway referral 2023
BSG/ACPGBI post-polypectomy surveillance 2020

codings.display: Encounter for screening for malignant neoplasm of colon

title: Breast cancer — 2-week referral criteria
description: Refer urgently (2-week pathway) any woman ≥30 with: unexplained breast lump (with or without pain), unilateral skin changes suspicious of breast cancer, change in shape, nipple discharge or eczema not improving. Consider urgent referral ≥50 with: nipple discharge, retraction, or other concerning unilateral nipple change. Refer non-urgently <30 with unexplained breast lump (with or without pain). Mammographic screening 50-71 every 3 years in UK; high-risk (BRCA1/2, TP53, family history) — earlier and more frequent surveillance with MRI in specialist breast clinic.

outcomes.summary: Breast lump or unilateral nipple change ≥30 — 2-week referral
outcomes.detail: Risk-stratified screening; specialist surveillance for BRCA/TP53/family history.

references.label: NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral 2015 (updated)
